title: Machine Learning on Robot Data

mentor.name: WEIGHT-6
mentor.character: Assumes every number you show it came from the training rows until you prove it did not.

summary: You will turn raw robot logs into features, then build nearest neighbour, logistic regression and tree classifiers by hand with numpy, plus least squares regression and behaviour cloning from teleop demonstrations. By the end you ship a bearing fault detector whose accuracy was measured on sessions the model never saw, with a threshold chosen from the cost of each error.

lessons.title: Rows, Columns and a Robot
lessons.goal: Build a feature matrix and a label vector from raw log rows and read their shapes.
lessons.theory:
Every machine learning method in this course eats the same two objects. `X` is a **feature matrix** with one row per example and one column per measured quantity, and `y` is a **label vector** with one entry per row of `X`. Nothing else. If you can put your robot data into that shape you can run every algorithm here on it.

On the Pattern Loft the examples come from a six axis arm. Joint 3 runs a harmonic drive and its controller logs motor current at 1 kHz. We cut that stream into windows of fixed length and reduce each window to a handful of numbers: that gives one row. The label says what state the joint was in during that window.

The shape is worth reading out loud every time you build it. `X.shape` returns `(n_rows, n_columns)` and `y.shape` returns `(n_rows,)`. The first number has to match. A mismatch there is the most common bug in a data pipeline, and it does not raise until three functions later when a distance calculation broadcasts into a matrix you never wanted.
lessons.task: Turn `rows` into a feature matrix with `X = np.array(rows)`, turn the label list into a vector with `np.array(labels)`, and print the shape of each along with `np.bincount(y)` so you can see how many examples each class has.
lessons.starter:
import numpy as np

rows = [
    [3.11, 1.02],
    [2.74, 0.88],
    [3.48, 1.71],
    [2.95, 1.44],
    [3.30, 1.66],
    [2.61, 0.79],
]
labels = [0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0]

# TODO: build the feature matrix and the label vector, then report both shapes
X = np.zeros((1, 1))
y = np.zeros(1, dtype=int)

print("features", X.shape)
print("labels", y.shape)
lessons.solution:
import numpy as np

rows = [
    [3.11, 1.02],
    [2.74, 0.88],
    [3.48, 1.71],
    [2.95, 1.44],
    [3.30, 1.66],
    [2.61, 0.79],
]
labels = [0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0]

X = np.array(rows)
y = np.array(labels)

print("features", X.shape)
print("labels", y.shape)
print("examples per class", np.bincount(y))
lessons.hint: `np.array` on a list of equal length lists gives you a two dimensional array directly, and `np.bincount(y)` counts how many times each integer label appears.

lessons.title: Parsing the Session File
lessons.goal: Read a comma separated robot log into a float feature matrix and an integer label vector.
lessons.theory:
Robot logs arrive as text. A controller writes one line per window, the fields are comma separated, and the first line names the columns. Python reads that with `csv.reader` from the standard library, which handles quoting and line endings that a naive `split` gets wrong.

The part that bites is types. Everything `csv.reader` gives you is a **string**, including the numbers. If you feed those strings straight into numpy you get an array of text and every arithmetic operation either fails or does something strange like concatenating. Convert while you parse, one call per field.

Keep the label out of the feature matrix. It sounds obvious written down and it is still the most expensive mistake in this course, because a model that can read the answer scores perfectly and teaches you nothing. Slice the label column off explicitly and never let it back in.
lessons.task: Parse `LOG` with `csv.reader`, skip the header, and build the feature rows from the first two fields as floats with `float(line[0])` plus the labels from the last field with `int(line[2])`. Build the matrix with `dtype=float` and print both shapes.
lessons.starter:
import csv
import io
import numpy as np

LOG = """rms_a,hf_a,state
3.11,1.02,0
2.74,0.88,0
3.48,1.71,1
2.95,1.44,1
3.30,1.66,1
2.61,0.79,0
"""

reader = csv.reader(io.StringIO(LOG))
header = next(reader)
print("columns", header)

# TODO: parse the remaining lines into numbers, features apart from the label
rows = []
labels = []
for line in reader:
    rows.append([0.0, 0.0])
    labels.append(0)

X = np.array(rows)
y = np.array(labels)
print("features", X.shape, "labels", y.shape, "first row", X[0])
lessons.solution:
import csv
import io
import numpy as np

LOG = """rms_a,hf_a,state
3.11,1.02,0
2.74,0.88,0
3.48,1.71,1
2.95,1.44,1
3.30,1.66,1
2.61,0.79,0
"""

reader = csv.reader(io.StringIO(LOG))
header = next(reader)
print("columns", header)

rows = []
labels = []
for line in reader:
    rows.append([float(line[0]), float(line[1])])
    labels.append(int(line[2]))

X = np.array(rows, dtype=float)
y = np.array(labels)
print("features", X.shape, "labels", y.shape, "first row", X[0])
print("column means", np.round(X.mean(axis=0), 3))
lessons.hint: Inside the loop every field is still a string, so convert each one as you take it and let the label stay an integer because `np.bincount` and the confusion matrix later both need integers.

lessons.title: Where the Labels Come From
lessons.goal: Label windows by comparing their start times against a logged fault interval.
lessons.theory:
Nobody hands you a labelled robot dataset. What you get is a stream of measurements and a maintenance note saying the joint was replaced on a certain date, or an operator log saying the arm was jammed between two timestamps. Turning that into a `y` vector is called **labelling** and it is where most of the honest work lives.

The usual mechanic is an interval test. Each window has a start time. If that start falls inside a known bad interval the window is class 1, otherwise class 0. In numpy that is one vectorized comparison over the whole array of start times, no loop needed, with the two halves joined by `&`.

Be suspicious of the edges. A window that straddles the moment the fault began contains both healthy and faulty signal, and whichever label you give it is half wrong. Serious pipelines drop those boundary windows rather than teach the model a contradiction.
lessons.task: Build a boolean mask that is true when a window start lies inside the interval using `(start >= FAULT_FROM) & (start < FAULT_TO)`, turn it into integer labels with `inside.astype(int)`, and print how many windows fell in each class.
lessons.starter:
import numpy as np

FAULT_FROM = 40.0
FAULT_TO = 70.0

start = np.arange(0.0, 100.0, 2.5)

# TODO: a window is class 1 only while its start sits inside the logged fault interval
inside = np.zeros(start.shape, dtype=bool)
y = np.zeros(start.shape[0], dtype=int)

print("windows", start.shape[0])
print("per class", np.bincount(y, minlength=2))
lessons.solution:
import numpy as np

FAULT_FROM = 40.0
FAULT_TO = 70.0

start = np.arange(0.0, 100.0, 2.5)

inside = (start >= FAULT_FROM) & (start < FAULT_TO)
y = inside.astype(int)

print("windows", start.shape[0])
print("per class", np.bincount(y, minlength=2))
print("first faulty window starts at", start[y == 1][0])
print("last faulty window starts at", start[y == 1][-1])
lessons.hint: Numpy needs `&` between the two comparisons, not the word `and`, and each comparison needs its own parentheses because `&` binds tighter than a comparison operator.

lessons.title: The Model That Only Remembers
lessons.goal: Show that a lookup table scores perfectly on the rows it was built from and no better than a coin on new rows.
lessons.theory:
Here is the trap the whole field is built around avoiding. Build a dictionary from every training row to its label. Ask it about a training row and it answers correctly every single time. **Accuracy 1.0.** It has learned nothing: it memorized.

The number that means something is accuracy on rows the model never saw. Split the data once, fit on one part, score on the other. If you score on the rows you fit on you are measuring memory, and memory is free. Every result in this course is reported on held out rows without exception, and when someone shows you a robot model with a suspiciously round accuracy this is the first question to ask.

The memorizer also shows what the failure looks like from outside: the model does not break, it answers confidently and at chance. Two numbers side by side, train and test, tell you which one you are looking at.
lessons.task: Fill the dictionary with one entry per training row by writing `memory[tuple(row)] = label` inside the loop, then score the table a second time over `zip(X_test, y_test)` and print that result under the caption `accuracy on rows it never saw` so the gap against the training score is visible.
lessons.starter:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
X = np.round(rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, (120, 2)), 4)
y = rng.integers(0, 2, 120)

X_train, y_train = X[:80], y[:80]
X_test, y_test = X[80:], y[80:]

memory = {}
# TODO: memorize every training row, then score the table on both sets

def lookup(row):
    return memory.get(tuple(row), 0)

on_train = np.mean([lookup(f) == e for f, e in zip(X_train, y_train)])
print("accuracy on rows it was built from", round(on_train, 3))
lessons.solution:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
X = np.round(rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, (120, 2)), 4)
y = rng.integers(0, 2, 120)

X_train, y_train = X[:80], y[:80]
X_test, y_test = X[80:], y[80:]

memory = {}
for row, label in zip(X_train, y_train):
    memory[tuple(row)] = label

def lookup(row):
    return memory.get(tuple(row), 0)

on_train = np.mean([lookup(f) == e for f, e in zip(X_train, y_train)])
on_test = np.mean([lookup(f) == e for f, e in zip(X_test, y_test)])

print("accuracy on rows it was built from", round(on_train, 3))
print("accuracy on rows it never saw", round(on_test, 3))
print("memorized entries", len(memory))
lessons.hint: A numpy row is not hashable so the dictionary key has to be the tuple version of it, and the second score is the same comprehension with the test pair in place of the training pair.

value: accuracy on rows it never saw

lessons.title: The Number You Have to Beat
lessons.goal: Compute the majority class baseline and compare a model against it instead of against zero.
lessons.theory:
An accuracy on its own is not a result. Accuracy of 0.95 sounds excellent until you learn that 95 percent of the windows in the log were healthy, in which case a constant predictor that always answers healthy scores the same 0.95 while being worth nothing.

The **majority baseline** is that constant predictor. Find the most common label in the training set, predict it for everything, and score it on the test set exactly the way you score a real model. That number is the floor. A model that does not clear it should be deleted, not tuned.

Write the baseline before you write the model. It costs three lines, it never breaks, and it is the only defence against reporting a number that a robot technician could have produced by saying nothing at all. Every project in this course prints its baseline next to its result.
lessons.task: Take the most common training label with `np.bincount(y_train).argmax()`, predict it for every test row, and print `baseline accuracy` next to the accuracy of the one rule model already written for you.
lessons.starter:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
healthy = rng.normal(1.0, 0.30, 260)
worn = rng.normal(1.9, 0.30, 60)
X = np.concatenate([healthy, worn])
y = np.concatenate([np.zeros(260, int), np.ones(60, int)])

order = rng.permutation(X.shape[0])
X, y = X[order], y[order]
X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test = X[:220], y[:220], X[220:], y[220:]

model = (X_test > 1.45).astype(int)
print("model accuracy", round(np.mean(model == y_test), 3))

# TODO: the constant predictor that always answers the most common training label
majority = -1
print("most common training label", majority)
lessons.solution:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
healthy = rng.normal(1.0, 0.30, 260)
worn = rng.normal(1.9, 0.30, 60)
X = np.concatenate([healthy, worn])
y = np.concatenate([np.zeros(260, int), np.ones(60, int)])

order = rng.permutation(X.shape[0])
X, y = X[order], y[order]
X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test = X[:220], y[:220], X[220:], y[220:]

model = (X_test > 1.45).astype(int)
print("model accuracy", round(np.mean(model == y_test), 3))

majority = np.bincount(y_train).argmax()
always = np.full(y_test.shape, majority)
print("most common training label", majority)
print("baseline accuracy", round(np.mean(always == y_test), 3))
lessons.hint: `np.bincount` counts each integer label and `.argmax()` gives the index of the biggest count, which is the label itself; `np.full(y_test.shape, majority)` then repeats it across the whole test set.

lessons.title: Cutting the Stream
lessons.goal: Slice a continuous current log into fixed length windows and drop the incomplete tail.
lessons.theory:
A machine learning row has to be a fixed length vector, and a current log is a stream of unknown length. The bridge between them is **windowing**: chop the stream into blocks of a fixed number of samples and let each block become one example.

The window length is a real engineering choice. Too short and a single bearing rotation does not fit inside it, so the feature you want is not present in the data. Too long and a fault that lasts half a second gets averaged away by three seconds of healthy signal. On joint 3, sampled at 1 kHz, 200 samples is 0.2 seconds and covers several revolutions of the output shaft.

Numpy does the cut with `reshape`, but reshape refuses to work unless the total size divides exactly. A 7.412 second log at 1 kHz gives 7412 samples, which is 37 whole windows with 12 samples left over. Trim the remainder before reshaping. Never pad it with zeros: a window that is half real signal and half zeros produces feature values that belong to no machine state at all.
lessons.task: Trim the log to a whole number of windows using `signal.size % WIN`, cut it with `reshape(-1, WIN)`, and print how many samples you threw away under the caption `discarded samples`.
lessons.starter:
import numpy as np

WIN = 200
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)

def stream(worn, blocks):
    parts = []
    for _ in range(blocks):
        load = np.exp(rng.uniform(np.log(0.4), np.log(2.0)))
        rough = (0.16 if worn else 0.08) * np.exp(rng.normal(0.0, 0.25))
        parts.append(load * 2.6 + rough * load * rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, WIN))
    return np.concatenate(parts)

signal = stream(False, 40)[:7412]
print("samples", signal.size)

# TODO: keep only whole windows, then cut the stream into rows
windows = signal.reshape(1, -1)

print("windows", windows.shape)
lessons.solution:
import numpy as np

WIN = 200
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)

def stream(worn, blocks):
    parts = []
    for _ in range(blocks):
        load = np.exp(rng.uniform(np.log(0.4), np.log(2.0)))
        rough = (0.16 if worn else 0.08) * np.exp(rng.normal(0.0, 0.25))
        parts.append(load * 2.6 + rough * load * rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, WIN))
    return np.concatenate(parts)

signal = stream(False, 40)[:7412]
print("samples", signal.size)

leftover = signal.size % WIN
usable = signal.size - leftover
windows = signal[:usable].reshape(-1, WIN)

print("windows", windows.shape)
print("discarded samples", leftover)
print("first window mean current", round(windows[0].mean(), 3))
lessons.hint: The remainder operator gives you exactly how many samples do not fit; subtract it from the size, slice up to there, and let the minus one in the reshape work out the row count for you.

lessons.title: The Feature That Says Nothing
lessons.goal: Compute per window mean and standard deviation and see which of the two responds to bearing wear.
lessons.theory:
The first two features anybody writes are the mean and the standard deviation of the window. With `axis=1` numpy computes them per row, giving one number per window instead of one number for the whole log.

On a motor current signal they carry completely different information. The **mean** is the average torque the joint was producing, which is set by the payload and the trajectory, not by the health of the bearing. The **standard deviation** is the size of the wobble around that average, and a worn bearing wobbles more.

Compare them in relative terms, not absolute. Mean current sits near 2.6 amps and spread near 0.08 amps, so a raw difference of 0.1 is nothing to the first and enormous to the second. Divide the worn average by the healthy average and subtract one: that gives the fractional change, and it is the only form in which two features measured in different sizes can be compared at all.
lessons.task: Compute one value per window for each log with `healthy.mean(axis=1)` and `healthy.std(axis=1)`, and the same two for the worn log, then print the fractional change of each feature between the two classes, ending with the line `spread changes by`.
lessons.starter:
import numpy as np

WIN = 200
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)

def stream(worn, blocks):
    parts = []
    for _ in range(blocks):
        load = np.exp(rng.uniform(np.log(0.4), np.log(2.0)))
        rough = (0.16 if worn else 0.08) * np.exp(rng.normal(0.0, 0.25))
        parts.append(load * 2.6 + rough * load * rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, WIN))
    return np.concatenate(parts)

healthy = stream(False, 60).reshape(-1, WIN)
worn = stream(True, 60).reshape(-1, WIN)

# TODO: one mean and one spread per window, for each log
h_mean = np.zeros(healthy.shape[0])
h_spread = np.zeros(healthy.shape[0])
w_mean = np.zeros(worn.shape[0])
w_spread = np.zeros(worn.shape[0])

print("healthy avg mean current", round(h_mean.mean(), 3), "avg spread", round(h_spread.mean(), 4))
print("worn    avg mean current", round(w_mean.mean(), 3), "avg spread", round(w_spread.mean(), 4))
lessons.solution:
import numpy as np

WIN = 200
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)

def stream(worn, blocks):
    parts = []
    for _ in range(blocks):
        load = np.exp(rng.uniform(np.log(0.4), np.log(2.0)))
        rough = (0.16 if worn else 0.08) * np.exp(rng.normal(0.0, 0.25))
        parts.append(load * 2.6 + rough * load * rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, WIN))
    return np.concatenate(parts)

healthy = stream(False, 60).reshape(-1, WIN)
worn = stream(True, 60).reshape(-1, WIN)

h_mean = healthy.mean(axis=1)
h_spread = healthy.std(axis=1)
w_mean = worn.mean(axis=1)
w_spread = worn.std(axis=1)

print("healthy avg mean current", round(h_mean.mean(), 3), "avg spread", round(h_spread.mean(), 4))
print("worn    avg mean current", round(w_mean.mean(), 3), "avg spread", round(w_spread.mean(), 4))
print("mean current changes by", round(w_mean.mean() / h_mean.mean() - 1.0, 3))
print("spread changes by", round(w_spread.mean() / h_spread.mean() - 1.0, 3))
lessons.hint: Without `axis=1` both calls collapse the whole matrix to a single scalar; with it you get one value per row, which is what a feature column is.

lessons.title: Root Mean Square
lessons.goal: Compute the RMS of a window and the AC only RMS after removing each window's own mean.
lessons.theory:
RMS is the square root of the mean of the squares, and for a current signal it is the value that actually heats the motor windings. It is the feature a thermal model wants, so it belongs in any dataset about a joint that gets hot.

There is a catch that ruins it as a health feature. Motor current on a loaded joint is mostly a constant offset with a small wobble on top. The square of that is dominated by the offset, so RMS comes back almost exactly equal to the mean and tells you about the payload rather than the bearing.

The fix is to remove each window's own mean before squaring, which leaves the **AC component**. Subtracting the per window mean on its own fails to broadcast, because a column of 40 values will not line up against a matrix of 40 by 200. You need `keepdims=True` so the mean keeps its second axis and numpy subtracts it row by row.
lessons.task: Build the AC part by subtracting the per window mean computed with `keepdims=True`, compute its RMS with `np.sqrt((ac ** 2).mean(axis=1))`, and print the plain RMS next to the plain mean plus the `ac rms average` so the difference is visible.
lessons.starter:
import numpy as np

WIN = 200
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)

def stream(worn, blocks):
    parts = []
    for _ in range(blocks):
        load = np.exp(rng.uniform(np.log(0.4), np.log(2.0)))
        rough = (0.16 if worn else 0.08) * np.exp(rng.normal(0.0, 0.25))
        parts.append(load * 2.6 + rough * load * rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, WIN))
    return np.concatenate(parts)

windows = stream(True, 40).reshape(-1, WIN)
plain = np.sqrt((windows ** 2).mean(axis=1))

# TODO: strip each window's own offset, then measure what is left
ac = windows
ac_rms = np.zeros(windows.shape[0])

print("plain rms of window 0", round(plain[0], 4))
print("ac rms of window 0", round(ac_rms[0], 4))
lessons.solution:
import numpy as np

WIN = 200
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)

def stream(worn, blocks):
    parts = []
    for _ in range(blocks):
        load = np.exp(rng.uniform(np.log(0.4), np.log(2.0)))
        rough = (0.16 if worn else 0.08) * np.exp(rng.normal(0.0, 0.25))
        parts.append(load * 2.6 + rough * load * rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, WIN))
    return np.concatenate(parts)

windows = stream(True, 40).reshape(-1, WIN)
plain = np.sqrt((windows ** 2).mean(axis=1))

ac = windows - windows.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)
ac_rms = np.sqrt((ac ** 2).mean(axis=1))

print("plain rms of window 0", round(plain[0], 4))
print("ac rms of window 0", round(ac_rms[0], 4))
print("plain rms vs mean current", round(plain.mean(), 4), round(windows.mean(), 4))
print("ac rms average", round(ac_rms.mean(), 4))
lessons.hint: Compare the plain RMS against the plain mean in the output: they land within a hundredth of each other, which is the proof that the offset was doing all the work.

lessons.title: The Spike That Breaks Peak to Peak
lessons.goal: Compare peak to peak against a percentile range on a window containing one contactor spike.
lessons.theory:
Peak to peak is the largest sample minus the smallest one. It is cheap, it needs no statistics, and it is the first thing a technician looks at on a scope. As a feature it has one fatal property: it depends on exactly two samples out of two hundred.

A robot cell is full of single sample events. A contactor closes, a welder fires two racks over, a ground loop picks up a switching supply, and one sample in your window jumps by four amps. Peak to peak reports that as a huge change in the machine state. It is not a change in the machine state, it is one bad sample.

The robust version is a **percentile range**: the value below which 95 percent of samples fall, minus the value below which 5 percent fall. Discarding the top and bottom five percent throws away the spike and keeps the shape of the distribution. It costs a sort and it does not lie to you.
lessons.task: Compute the robust range of every window with `np.percentile(windows, 95, axis=1) - np.percentile(windows, 5, axis=1)` and the same for the spiked copy, then print how much each measure moved, ending with the line `robust range grew by`.
lessons.starter:
import numpy as np

WIN = 200
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)

def stream(worn, blocks):
    parts = []
    for _ in range(blocks):
        load = np.exp(rng.uniform(np.log(0.4), np.log(2.0)))
        rough = (0.16 if worn else 0.08) * np.exp(rng.normal(0.0, 0.25))
        parts.append(load * 2.6 + rough * load * rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, WIN))
    return np.concatenate(parts)

windows = stream(False, 20).reshape(-1, WIN)
spiked = windows.copy()
spiked[0, 90] = spiked[0, 90] + 4.0

clean_ptp = windows[0].max() - windows[0].min()
spiked_ptp = spiked[0].max() - spiked[0].min()

# TODO: the range that ignores the extremes, on both versions of the window
clean_range = 0.0
spiked_range = 0.0

print("peak to peak clean", round(clean_ptp, 3), "spiked", round(spiked_ptp, 3))
print("robust range clean", round(clean_range, 3), "spiked", round(spiked_range, 3))
lessons.solution:
import numpy as np

WIN = 200
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)

def stream(worn, blocks):
    parts = []
    for _ in range(blocks):
        load = np.exp(rng.uniform(np.log(0.4), np.log(2.0)))
        rough = (0.16 if worn else 0.08) * np.exp(rng.normal(0.0, 0.25))
        parts.append(load * 2.6 + rough * load * rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, WIN))
    return np.concatenate(parts)

windows = stream(False, 20).reshape(-1, WIN)
spiked = windows.copy()
spiked[0, 90] = spiked[0, 90] + 4.0

clean_ptp = windows[0].max() - windows[0].min()
spiked_ptp = spiked[0].max() - spiked[0].min()

clean_all = np.percentile(windows, 95, axis=1) - np.percentile(windows, 5, axis=1)
spiked_all = np.percentile(spiked, 95, axis=1) - np.percentile(spiked, 5, axis=1)
clean_range = clean_all[0]
spiked_range = spiked_all[0]

print("peak to peak clean", round(clean_ptp, 3), "spiked", round(spiked_ptp, 3))
print("robust range clean", round(clean_range, 3), "spiked", round(spiked_range, 3))
print("peak to peak grew by", round(spiked_ptp - clean_ptp, 3))
print("robust range grew by", round(spiked_range - clean_range, 3))

lessons.title: The Chatter Band
lessons.goal: Measure high frequency energy in a window as the mean absolute sample to sample difference.
lessons.theory:
A worn bearing does not change the average current, it adds **fast** content: small, rapid deviations riding on top of the smooth torque demand. Standard deviation counts all deviation regardless of speed, so a slow payload ramp inflates it just as much as real chatter does.

The cheapest separator between slow and fast is the difference between consecutive samples. A signal that drifts slowly has tiny sample to sample steps even when its total swing is large. A signal with high frequency content has large steps even when its total swing is small. Averaging the absolute value of the differences over the window gives one number for how jagged it is.

This is a crude high pass filter and it is enough here. The signals course builds the proper FIR version. What matters for a dataset is that the feature responds to the physical thing you care about and stays flat when the thing you do not care about changes.
lessons.task: Compute the chatter feature with `np.mean(np.abs(np.diff(healthy, axis=1)), axis=1)` and with `np.abs(np.diff(worn, axis=1))` averaged the same way, then print the class averages of chatter next to the class averages of the plain spread and finish with the line `chatter ratio worn over healthy`.

        parts.append(load * 2.6 + rough * load * rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, WIN))

lessons.title: Counting Sign Changes
lessons.goal: Compute the zero crossing rate of the AC part and separate two windows that have identical spread.
lessons.theory:
The **zero crossing rate** counts how often a signal changes sign, divided by the window length. It is a frequency estimate that needs no transform: a fast signal crosses zero often, a slow one rarely.

It earns its place because it sees something spread cannot. Broadband bearing noise and a stick slip limit cycle can have exactly the same standard deviation while one wanders across zero on every second sample and the other crosses four times in the whole window. Any feature built on amplitude alone reports those two states as identical.

On a motor current it only means something after you remove the offset. A joint holding 2.6 amps never crosses zero at all, so the raw rate is zero for every window and the feature is a constant. The implementation also avoids comparing floats against zero: `np.signbit` returns a boolean array that is true for negatives, the difference of that boolean array is non zero exactly where the sign flipped, and counting those flips needs no epsilon and no special case for a sample that lands on zero.
lessons.task: Write the counter with `np.count_nonzero(np.diff(np.signbit(ac), axis=1), axis=1)` divided by `WIN`, run it on both blocks, and also print the same rate computed on the raw broadband block under the caption `same feature without removing the offset`.

WIN = 200
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)

broadband = 2.6 + 0.13 * rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, (60, WIN))
stick_slip = 2.6 + 0.184 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 22.0 * t) + 0.01 * rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, (60, WIN))

def rate(block):
    ac = block - block.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    # TODO: count how many times the AC part flips sign, then turn it into a rate
    flips = np.zeros(block.shape[0], dtype=int)

print("crossing rate broadband", round(rate(broadband).mean(), 4))
print("crossing rate stick slip", round(rate(stick_slip).mean(), 4))

import numpy as np

WIN = 200
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
t = np.arange(WIN) / 1000.0

broadband = 2.6 + 0.13 * rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, (60, WIN))
stick_slip = 2.6 + 0.184 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 22.0 * t) + 0.01 * rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, (60, WIN))

lessons.title: Dividing Out the Payload
lessons.goal: Build a ratio feature and measure that it no longer tracks the payload the way its parts do.
lessons.theory:
Chatter grows with wear, and it also grows with load, because a heavier payload drives more current through everything including the noise. A robot lifting a heavy part with a perfect bearing can produce more chatter than the same robot lifting nothing with a ruined one. The feature is **confounded**.

The cure is a ratio. Chatter divided by RMS cancels the common load factor and leaves the part that is about the bearing. In physical terms you have moved from an absolute measurement to a relative one: not how much noise, but how much noise per amp.

You can check whether it worked without any model at all. Compute the correlation between each feature and the known load. A feature doing its job on machine health should correlate weakly with load, and a confounded one correlates strongly. Correlation of a pair of arrays is one call away and it is the cheapest audit in this course.
lessons.task: Write `ratio = chatter / rms` and then print `np.corrcoef(ratio, load)[0, 1]` under its own caption, so the drop against the two correlations already on screen is visible.

    parts.append(load_now * 2.6 + rough * load_now * rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, WIN))
    loads.append(load_now)

lessons.title: The Feature That Reads the Clock
lessons.goal: Show that a window index feature scores perfectly on one session and lands below the baseline on the next.
lessons.theory:
Here is a feature that passes every test you can run inside one log and destroys the model in the field. In session A the bearing failed halfway through, so every window after number 40 is faulty. The window index therefore predicts the label perfectly. A classifier finds it instantly, because it is the cleanest signal in the table.

It has learned when the recording was made, not what a bad bearing sounds like. Session B is a different cell where the bearing was replaced during the recording, so the faulty windows sit at the **start**. The rule fitted on session A does not merely degrade there, it comes out inverted and scores far below the majority baseline. This is **leakage**: information that correlates with the label inside your dataset and carries none of the physics.

Timestamps, row numbers, file order and sensor identifiers are the usual carriers. The test is always the same question: would this number still mean the same thing on a robot that is not this one, in a session that is not this one. If not, it does not go in the feature matrix.
lessons.task: Fit the clock threshold on session A by taking `index_a[y_a == 1].min()`, apply that same rule to session B, and print both scores under the two captions already used, ending with `clock rule on session B`.
lessons.starter:
import numpy as np

WIN = 200
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)

def stream(worn, blocks):
    parts = []
    for _ in range(blocks):
        load = np.exp(rng.uniform(np.log(0.4), np.log(2.0)))
        rough = (0.16 if worn else 0.08) * np.exp(rng.normal(0.0, 0.25))
        parts.append(load * 2.6 + rough * load * rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, WIN))
    return np.concatenate(parts)

def session(pattern, seed):
    global rng
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    blocks, labels = [], []
    for worn, count in pattern:
        blocks.append(stream(worn, count).reshape(-1, WIN))
        labels.extend([1 if worn else 0] * count)
    block = np.vstack(blocks)
    y = np.array(labels)
    chatter = np.mean(np.abs(np.diff(block, axis=1)), axis=1)
    rms = np.sqrt((block ** 2).mean(axis=1))
    return np.arange(y.size), chatter / rms, y

index_a, ratio_a, y_a = session([(False, 40), (True, 40)], 21)
index_b, ratio_b, y_b = session([(True, 30), (False, 50)], 22)

cut = ratio_a[y_a == 1].mean() * 0.5 + ratio_a[y_a == 0].mean() * 0.5
print("chatter rule on session A", round(np.mean((ratio_a > cut).astype(int) == y_a), 3))
print("chatter rule on session B", round(np.mean((ratio_b > cut).astype(int) == y_b), 3))
print("majority baseline on session B", round(np.mean(y_b == np.bincount(y_b).argmax()), 3))

# TODO: fit the same kind of rule on the window number and carry it to session B
clock_cut = 0

lessons.title: Is This Feature Worth Having
lessons.goal: Rank candidate features by the accuracy of the best single threshold measured on held out windows.
lessons.theory:
Before any classifier exists you can already ask how much each column is worth. Sweep a threshold across one feature, try both directions, keep the best accuracy. That number is what a one rule model would achieve using that column alone.

Measure it on windows the sweep did not touch. Choosing the threshold is fitting, and a threshold chosen on the same rows it is scored on is optimistic by several points on a small set. The habit costs one extra slice and it is the difference between a ranking you can trust and a ranking you cannot.

Read the result as a floor, not as a verdict. A column at 0.55 alone can still be valuable in combination, which is the entire point of the ratio you built two lessons ago: chatter alone and RMS alone are both mediocre and their quotient is strong. What the ranking does tell you is which columns are pure noise, and those you delete.

lessons.title: The Column That Shouts
lessons.goal: Show that an unscaled column with large units decides every nearest neighbour on its own.
lessons.theory:
Nearest neighbour, and every other method that measures distance, adds up the squared differences of all columns. That sum has no idea what the columns mean. A difference of 40 in motor speed measured in rpm contributes sixteen hundred to the sum, and a difference of 0.6 in high frequency energy measured in decibels contributes 0.36.

So the loud column wins. If spindle speed happens to be recorded in rpm and your health features are in decibels, the model is a spindle speed model wearing a costume. The clue that this has happened is that dropping the useful columns changes nothing, because they were never being consulted.

The fix is **scaling**: put every column on a comparable footing before measuring distance. This lesson only shows you the damage. The next one builds the scaler. The classifier used here is given to you already written, because chapter 3 is where you build it yourself.
lessons.task: Score the same classifier twice on the same rows, once on the raw matrix and once after dividing every column by `spreads = X_train.std(axis=0)`, and print the second result under the caption `accuracy on scaled columns`.
lessons.starter:
import numpy as np

def bench(n, worn, rng):
    load = rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, n)
    rms_db = 3.0 + 0.9 * load + rng.normal(0.0, 0.15, n)
    hf_db = (1.6 if worn else 1.0) + 0.9 * load + rng.normal(0.0, 0.15, n)
    return np.column_stack([rms_db, hf_db])

def nearest(X_train, y_train, X_query, k=7):
    out = []
    for row in X_query:
        gap = ((X_train - row) ** 2).sum(axis=1)
        out.append(np.bincount(y_train[np.argsort(gap)[:k]]).argmax())
    return np.array(out)

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
X = np.vstack([bench(200, False, rng), bench(200, True, rng)])
y = np.concatenate([np.zeros(200, int), np.ones(200, int)])
speed = rng.normal(1800.0, 120.0, 400).reshape(-1, 1)
X = np.hstack([X, speed])

order = np.random.default_rng(2).permutation(400)
X_train, y_train = X[order[:300]], y[order[:300]]
X_test, y_test = X[order[300:]], y[order[300:]]

print("column spreads", np.round(X_train.std(axis=0), 2))
raw = nearest(X_train, y_train, X_test)
print("accuracy on raw columns", round(np.mean(raw == y_test), 3))

# TODO: give every column the same weight in the distance, then score again

lessons.title: Statistics Belong to the Training Set
lessons.goal: Standardize a dataset using the training mean and spread and apply the same numbers to the test rows.
lessons.theory:
Standardizing means subtracting a mean and dividing by a standard deviation so that a column comes out centred on zero with a spread of one. The question that decides whether you did it right is: **whose** mean and whose standard deviation.

They have to be the training set's. In deployment the scaler runs on one window at a time, arriving from a robot, and there is no set of future rows to average. Whatever numbers the scaler holds must have been computed before that window existed. Fitting on the training rows is the only version of the operation that can also run in the field.

The visible consequence is a good habit to build. After scaling, the training columns come out at mean 0.000 and spread 1.000 exactly, and the test columns come out near those values but not equal to them. That small mismatch is not a bug, it is the proof that the scaler never saw the test rows. A test set that comes out at exactly zero is the fingerprint of a leak.

lessons.title: One Spike Ruins Min Max
lessons.goal: Compare min max scaling with and without a single outlier row and measure how far the normal rows get squashed.
lessons.theory:
Min max scaling maps a column into the range zero to one by subtracting the minimum and dividing by the range. It is popular because the output range is guaranteed, which matters when the next stage is a neural network or a fixed point implementation on a microcontroller.

It is also the least robust thing in this chapter, for the same reason peak to peak was: it depends on exactly two rows. One window recorded while a contactor arced can sit ten decibels above everything else. That single row becomes 1.0, and the entire real population is compressed into the bottom eight percent of the range where every distance between real rows has been reduced by a factor of twelve.

Standardizing is the safer default because the mean and the standard deviation are computed over all rows, so one outlier moves them a little instead of defining them entirely. Use min max when a bounded range is a hard requirement, and clip the extremes before you do.

lessons.title: The Leak in the Preparation Step
lessons.goal: Select the best feature column using every row and see a pure noise dataset report accuracy far above chance.
lessons.theory:
This dataset has three thousand columns of pure noise and a label drawn by coin flip. There is nothing to learn. Any honest pipeline has to come back at the baseline, and if yours does not, the pipeline is broken rather than clever.

The break happens in the **preparation** step. Picking the column that correlates best with the label is fitting, exactly as much as training a classifier is fitting. Do it over all the rows and the column you pick was chosen partly because it happens to line up with the test labels, so the test set can no longer measure anything. With three thousand candidates, some column lines up beautifully by luck alone.

The rule is that every decision informed by the labels happens inside the training rows. Column selection, scaler statistics, outlier removal, resampling to balance the classes, the choice of window length. Split first, then prepare. If you find yourself writing a preparation step before the split, that is the moment to stop.
lessons.task: Call the selector twice, once as `pick(np.arange(N))` and once over the training rows only, score the column each version picked on the untouched test rows, and print the second result under the caption `column chosen with training rows only`.
lessons.starter:
import numpy as np

N, COLS = 60, 3000
rng = np.random.default_rng(31)
X = rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, (N, COLS))
y = rng.integers(0, 2, N)
train, test = np.arange(30), np.arange(30, N)

def pick(rows):
    block = X[rows]
    zx = (block - block.mean(axis=0)) / block.std(axis=0)
    zy = (y[rows] - y[rows].mean()) / y[rows].std()
    return int(np.argmax(np.abs((zx * zy[:, None]).sum(axis=0))))

def score(col):
    cut = X[train, col].mean()
    sign = 1 if X[train, col][y[train] == 1].mean() > cut else -1
    return np.mean((X[test, col] * sign > cut * sign).astype(int) == y[test])

# TODO: pick the column the leaky way and the honest way, then score both
print("baseline", round(max(np.bincount(y[test])) / test.size, 3))

import numpy as np

N, COLS = 60, 3000
rng = np.random.default_rng(31)
X = rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, (N, COLS))
y = rng.integers(0, 2, N)
train, test = np.arange(30), np.arange(30, N)

def pick(rows):
    block = X[rows]
    zx = (block - block.mean(axis=0)) / block.std(axis=0)
    zy = (y[rows] - y[rows].mean()) / y[rows].std()
    return int(np.argmax(np.abs((zx * zy[:, None]).sum(axis=0))))

lessons.title: The Seed Is Part of the Result
lessons.goal: Reproduce a shuffled split from its seed and show that a different seed moves the reported accuracy.
lessons.theory:
A split has to be shuffled. Robot logs arrive in time order and often in class order too, so slicing the first seventy percent hands you a training set made entirely of healthy windows. Shuffling with a permutation fixes that.

Shuffling has to be reproducible. `np.random.default_rng(5)` builds a generator whose stream depends only on the seed, so the same seed produces the same permutation on any machine, on any day. Without it, the accuracy you report cannot be checked by anyone, including you tomorrow.

And the seed is part of the result. Change it and the accuracy moves, sometimes by several points on a small test set, because a different set of rows landed on the test side. That variation is not noise you should hide, it is a measurement of how uncertain your single number is. Chapter 7 turns it into an error bar.
lessons.task: Build the permutation for a given seed with `np.random.default_rng(seed).permutation(400)`, print the first six indices for seed 5 twice and for seed 6 once, and then loop `for seed in (5, 6):` again to print the test accuracy under each.
lessons.hint: The two lines printed for seed 5 have to come out identical and the line for seed 6 has to differ, which is the whole point of naming the seed in the report.

lessons.title: Keeping the Rare Class in Both Halves
lessons.goal: Compare how many fault rows a plain shuffle leaves in the test set against a stratified split.
lessons.theory:
Faults are rare. A log with four percent faulty windows is a healthy dataset by industrial standards, and it is a trap for a plain shuffle. Shuffle three hundred rows with twelve faults, take sixty of them for testing, and the expected number of faults on the test side is under three. Some seeds give you one.

A test set with one fault in it cannot measure fault detection. Recall is either 0.0 or 1.0 and both numbers are meaningless. Worse, the training set for that seed is missing a large fraction of the examples of the class you actually care about.

A **stratified** split fixes the proportion instead of leaving it to luck. Shuffle within each class separately and take the same fraction from each, then join the pieces. The test set then holds the same class mix as the full dataset every time, and the only thing the seed changes is which particular rows.
lessons.task: Write the stratified version so it shuffles the indices of each class separately and takes the same fraction of each, then print how many faults land in the test set for eight different seeds under the caption `stratified shuffle`.
lessons.starter:
import numpy as np

def bench(n, worn, rng):
    load = rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, n)
    rms_db = 3.0 + 0.9 * load + rng.normal(0.0, 0.15, n)
    hf_db = (1.6 if worn else 1.0) + 0.9 * load + rng.normal(0.0, 0.15, n)
    return np.column_stack([rms_db, hf_db])

rng = np.random.default_rng(8)
X = np.vstack([bench(288, False, rng), bench(12, True, rng)])
y = np.concatenate([np.zeros(288, int), np.ones(12, int)])
TEST = 60

def plain(seed):
    order = np.random.default_rng(seed).permutation(y.size)
    return order[:TEST]

def stratified(seed):
    gen = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    # TODO: take the same fraction out of each class instead of out of the pile
    return gen.permutation(y.size)[:TEST]

print("faults in the whole set", int(y.sum()), "of", y.size)
print("plain shuffle     ", [int(y[plain(s)].sum()) for s in range(8)])

import numpy as np

def bench(n, worn, rng):
    load = rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, n)
    rms_db = 3.0 + 0.9 * load + rng.normal(0.0, 0.15, n)
    hf_db = (1.6 if worn else 1.0) + 0.9 * load + rng.normal(0.0, 0.15, n)
    return np.column_stack([rms_db, hf_db])

rng = np.random.default_rng(8)
X = np.vstack([bench(288, False, rng), bench(12, True, rng)])
y = np.concatenate([np.zeros(288, int), np.ones(12, int)])
TEST = 60

def plain(seed):
    order = np.random.default_rng(seed).permutation(y.size)
    return order[:TEST]

def stratified(seed):
    gen = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    share = TEST / y.size
    picked = []
    for label in (0, 1):
        rows = np.flatnonzero(y == label)
        gen.shuffle(rows)
        picked.append(rows[:int(round(share * rows.size))])
    return np.concatenate(picked)

print("faults in the whole set", int(y.sum()), "of", y.size)
print("plain shuffle     ", [int(y[plain(s)].sum()) for s in range(8)])
print("stratified shuffle", [int(y[stratified(s)].sum()) for s in range(8)])
print("test set sizes", [int(stratified(s).size) for s in range(8)])
lessons.hint: `np.flatnonzero(y == label)` gives the row numbers of one class; shuffle that list, take its share, and concatenate the two pieces at the end.

lessons.title: Windows That Overlap Are Not Independent
lessons.goal: Compare a shuffled split against a split by time on overlapping windows cut from the same two recordings.
lessons.theory:
Overlapping windows are standard practice: a hop shorter than the window length gives you more rows out of the same recording. Two neighbouring windows then share most of their samples, so their feature vectors are nearly the same point.

Shuffle those rows and you have put near duplicates on both sides of the split. Every test window has a twin sitting in the training set, and a nearest neighbour model looks it up rather than generalizing. The reported accuracy measures how similar a window is to itself.

Split by **time** instead: the first part of each recording trains, the last part tests, and no window straddles the boundary. On this pair of recordings the shuffled split reports a number well above the honest one, and the honest one is close to the coin flip that the data deserves, because the two roughness levels here differ by eight percent and there is almost nothing to find.
lessons.task: Build the honest split with `by_time_train = np.concatenate` over the first 70 percent of the rows of each recording and its mirror for the rest, then print the result under the caption `split by time says` next to the baseline.
lessons.starter:
import numpy as np

WIN, HOP = 64, 8

def record(worn, seed, n=12000):
    gen = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    walk = np.repeat(np.cumsum(gen.normal(0, 1, n // 400 + 2)), 400)[:n]
    walk = 0.22 * (walk - walk.mean()) / walk.std()
    load = np.exp(walk)
    return load * 2.6 + (0.13 if worn else 0.12) * load * gen.normal(0, 1, n)

def cut(signal):
    starts = np.arange(0, signal.size - WIN + 1, HOP)
    block = np.stack([signal[s:s + WIN] for s in starts])
    ac = block - block.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    return np.column_stack([block.mean(axis=1), np.sqrt((ac ** 2).mean(axis=1)),
                            np.mean(np.abs(np.diff(block, axis=1)), axis=1)])

def nearest(X_train, y_train, X_query):
    out = []
    for row in X_query:
        gap = ((X_train - row) ** 2).sum(axis=1)
        out.append(y_train[int(np.argmin(gap))])
    return np.array(out)

A, B = cut(record(False, 5)), cut(record(True, 6))
X = np.vstack([A, B])
y = np.concatenate([np.zeros(len(A), int), np.ones(len(B), int)])
X = (X - X.mean(axis=0)) / X.std(axis=0)

order = np.random.default_rng(0).permutation(len(X))
keep = int(0.7 * len(X))
shuffled = np.mean(nearest(X[order[:keep]], y[order[:keep]], X[order[keep:]]) == y[order[keep:]])
print("shuffled split says", round(shuffled, 3))

# TODO: train on the early part of each recording and test on the late part

X = np.vstack([A, B])

lessons.title: Never Split a Robot
lessons.goal: Compare a row level split against holding out whole robots when each unit has its own sensor offset.
lessons.theory:
Eight arms of the same model, four healthy and four with a worn joint. Each arm has its own current sensor with its own offset, a couple of decibels either way, fixed for that unit and completely unrelated to its health.

Split the rows at random and every arm appears on both sides. The model does not need to learn anything about bearings: it learns eight little clusters and the label attached to each. The accuracy comes back near perfect and the moment you install it on the ninth arm it produces nonsense, because that arm's offset lands somewhere the model has never been.

The honest split holds out **whole groups**. Train on six arms, test on the two nobody trained on, and the number you get is the one that describes a new installation. It will be much lower. That is not the split being unfair, that is the earlier number having been false.
lessons.task: Build the group split with `np.isin(group, [6, 7])` for the test side and its negation for training, then print that score under the caption `held out arms say` next to the baseline of those arms.
lessons.starter:
import numpy as np

def bench(n, worn, rng):
    load = rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, n)
    rms_db = 3.0 + 0.9 * load + rng.normal(0.0, 0.15, n)
    hf_db = (1.6 if worn else 1.0) + 0.9 * load + rng.normal(0.0, 0.15, n)
    return np.column_stack([rms_db, hf_db])

def nearest(X_train, y_train, X_query, k=7):
    out = []
    for row in X_query:
        gap = ((X_train - row) ** 2).sum(axis=1)
        out.append(np.bincount(y_train[np.argsort(gap)[:k]]).argmax())
    return np.array(out)

rng = np.random.default_rng(12)
ROBOTS, PER = 8, 60
rows, labels, groups = [], [], []
for unit in range(ROBOTS):
    worn = unit % 2
    offset = rng.normal(0.0, 1.2, 2)
    block = bench(PER, worn, rng)
    block[:, 1] = block[:, 1] - 1.3 * worn + 0.30 * worn
    rows.append(block + offset)
    labels.append(np.full(PER, worn))
    groups.append(np.full(PER, unit))

X = np.vstack(rows)
y = np.concatenate(labels)
group = np.concatenate(groups)
X = (X - X.mean(axis=0)) / X.std(axis=0)

order = np.random.default_rng(1).permutation(y.size)
keep = int(0.75 * y.size)
by_row = nearest(X[order[:keep]], y[order[:keep]], X[order[keep:]], 5)
print("row level split says", round(np.mean(by_row == y[order[keep:]]), 3))

# TODO: keep two whole arms out of the training set and score on those

lessons.title: The Set You Choose On Is Not the Set You Report
lessons.goal: Measure how much the winning validation score overstates the test score across twenty splits.
lessons.theory:
You have eight candidate values of k and one validation set. You score all eight, take the best, and report that number. It is too high, and it is too high for a reason that has nothing to do with leakage: the best of eight noisy measurements is biased upward, because whichever candidate got lucky on those particular rows is the one you kept.

The cure is a third slice. **Train** fits the model, **validation** chooses between models, and **test** is opened once, at the end, to produce the number that goes in the report. Every time you look at the test set to decide something, it stops being a test set and becomes a second validation set.

The size of the effect is worth measuring rather than believing. Repeat the whole protocol over twenty different splits and average the gap between the winner's validation score and its test score. It comes out small here and it is reliably on the optimistic side, and it grows with the number of candidates you try.
lessons.task: Inside the loop over the twenty splits, score every k on the validation slice, keep the winner, score that same k on the test slice, and print the `mean test score of that winner`, the mean optimism, and the count of `splits where validation beat test`.

import numpy as np

def bench(n, worn, rng):
    load = rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, n)
    rms_db = 3.0 + 0.9 * load + rng.normal(0.0, 0.15, n)
    hf_db = (1.6 if worn else 1.0) + 0.9 * load + rng.normal(0.0, 0.15, n)
    return np.column_stack([rms_db, hf_db])

def nearest(X_train, y_train, X_query, k=7):
    out = []
    for row in X_query:
        gap = ((X_train - row) ** 2).sum(axis=1)
        out.append(np.bincount(y_train[np.argsort(gap)[:k]]).argmax())
    return np.array(out)

rng = np.random.default_rng(21)
X = np.vstack([bench(300, False, rng), bench(300, True, rng)])
y = np.concatenate([np.zeros(300, int), np.ones(300, int)])
KS = (1, 3, 5, 9, 15, 25, 41, 61)

won, checked = [], []
for seed in range(20):
    order = np.random.default_rng(seed).permutation(600)
    train, valid, test = order[:360], order[360:480], order[480:]
    scores = [np.mean(nearest(X[train], y[train], X[valid], k) == y[valid]) for k in KS]
    best = int(np.argmax(scores))
    won.append(scores[best])
    checked.append(np.mean(nearest(X[train], y[train], X[test], KS[best]) == y[test]))

gaps = np.array(won) - np.array(checked)
print("candidates per split", len(KS))
print("mean winning validation score", round(float(np.mean(won)), 4))
print("mean test score of that winner", round(float(np.mean(checked)), 4))
print("mean optimism", round(float(gaps.mean()), 4))
print("splits where validation beat test", int(np.sum(gaps > 0)), "of", gaps.size)

lessons.title: How Far Apart Are Two Windows
lessons.goal: Compute the squared Euclidean distance from one query row to every training row without a loop.
lessons.theory:
Nearest neighbour needs one primitive: the distance from a query row to every row of the training set. In two dimensions that is the ordinary straight line distance, and in eight it is the same formula with more terms.

Numpy does it by **broadcasting**. Subtracting a row of shape `(2,)` from a matrix of shape `(420, 2)` lines the row up against every row of the matrix and returns a `(420, 2)` array of differences. Square that and sum along `axis=1` and you have 420 distances in one expression, with no Python loop over the training set.

Skip the square root. You only ever compare distances against each other, and the square root is monotonic, so it changes none of the orderings and costs one pass over the array. Every distance in this chapter is a squared distance and the code says so in its name.
lessons.task: Fill in the body so it returns `((X_train - row) ** 2).sum(axis=1)`, then print the shape of the result, the `three smallest distances` and the labels of those three closest training rows.

lessons.title: The Closest Window Wins
lessons.goal: Build a one nearest neighbour classifier and score it on held out rows.
lessons.theory:
One nearest neighbour is the smallest complete classifier there is. For a query row, find the training row closest to it and answer with that row's label. There is no training step: fitting means keeping the data.

It is a serious method, not a toy. On a fault detection problem with clean features it is often within a couple of points of anything fancier, and it needs no assumption about the shape of the boundary between classes. Its weaknesses are elsewhere: it stores every example, it slows down as the dataset grows, and it is defenceless against a badly scaled column, which is why the previous chapter came first.

`np.argmin` gives you the position of the smallest distance, and indexing the training labels with that position gives the answer. One line per query row.

lessons.title: A Perfect Score Means You Asked the Wrong Question
lessons.goal: Score one nearest neighbour on its own training rows and on held out rows in the same run.
lessons.theory:
Ask one nearest neighbour about a row that is in its training set and the closest row is that row itself, at distance zero. It answers with that row's own label, every time. Training accuracy is exactly **1.000** and it is a property of the algorithm, not a measurement of anything.

This is the clearest possible instance of the rule from chapter 0, and it is worth running once with your own hands so the number stops being an abstraction. Every method in this course can do a weaker version of the same thing. A tree deep enough puts one leaf under each training row. A regression with as many parameters as rows passes through all of them.

So the diagnosis is never the value of the training score, it is the **gap**. A small gap means the model is limited by the problem. A large gap means it is limited by memorization. One nearest neighbour shows you the extreme case: the gap is the entire distance between 1.000 and the truth.

lessons.title: Asking the Nearest Five
lessons.goal: Extend the classifier to take a majority vote among the k closest training rows.
lessons.theory:
One neighbour is one witness. If that witness happens to be a mislabelled window or a rare outlier, the answer is wrong and there is nothing to outvote it. Asking the **k** closest rows and taking the majority makes the classifier tolerate a bad neighbour or two.

The implementation stays short. `np.argsort` orders the distances, the first k positions are the closest rows, `np.bincount` counts how many of each label they carry, and `argmax` picks the winner. For two classes with k odd there is never a tie.

What you gain is smoothness. Where k is 1 the boundary between classes wraps around every individual training row, including the ones that sit deep inside the other class. Raising k pulls the boundary straight and stops it chasing single points, and pushing it too far starts erasing real structure. The next lesson measures where that turn happens.
lessons.task: Complete the vote with `np.bincount(y_train[np.argsort(gap)[:k]]).argmax()` and close with `for k in (1, 15):` printing the accuracy of each on the same test rows.

lessons.title: Choosing k Without Cheating
lessons.goal: Sweep k over a validation slice, pick the winner there, and report its score on the untouched test slice.
lessons.theory:
k is a **hyperparameter**: a number you choose rather than one the data fits for you. Choosing it is a fitting operation, so it needs its own slice of data, and reporting the score of the winner on that same slice gives you the optimistic number chapter 2 measured.

The protocol is the one from that chapter, now applied for real. Train holds the neighbours. Validation ranks the candidate values of k. Test is opened once, with the winner, at the end. Three slices, three jobs, no overlap.

Watch the shape of the sweep rather than its peak. Accuracy usually climbs quickly from k equal to 1, sits on a wide plateau, then falls once k gets large enough that the vote reaches across the whole dataset. Any value on the plateau is fine, and a peak that is one point above its neighbours is noise rather than a discovery.

import numpy as np

def bench(n, worn, rng):

    hf_db = (1.6 if worn else 1.0) + 0.9 * load + rng.normal(0.0, 0.15, n)

def vote(X_train, y_train, X_query, k):

        out.append(np.bincount(y_train[np.argsort(gap)[:k]]).argmax())

lessons.title: A Vote Weighted by Distance
lessons.goal: Replace the plain majority with a vote where each neighbour counts one over its distance.
lessons.theory:
A plain vote treats the closest neighbour and the fifteenth closest as equals. When a query lands in the middle of a dense cluster that is fine. When it lands out at the edge, where the fifteenth neighbour is four times further away than the first, it is not.

Weighting by `1 / (distance + eps)` fixes it. Near neighbours dominate, far ones still speak but quietly, and the classifier degrades gracefully as k grows instead of drowning the local evidence. The epsilon is there because a query that coincides exactly with a training row would otherwise divide by zero.

Adding the weights per class instead of counting rows needs one small change: instead of a bin count, sum the weights of the neighbours belonging to each label and compare the two sums. That also removes the tie problem, because two float sums almost never land on exactly the same value.
lessons.task: Compute the weights as `1.0 / (np.sqrt(gap[near]) + 1e-9)`, add them up per class, answer with the heavier class, and print the result under the caption `weighted vote at k` next to the plain vote at the same k.

    load = rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, n)
    rms_db = 3.0 + 0.9 * load + rng.normal(0.0, 0.15, n)
    hf_db = (1.6 if worn else 1.0) + 0.9 * load + rng.normal(0.0, 0.15, n)

def dataset(seed, n=300):

    X = np.vstack([bench(n, False, gen), bench(n, True, gen)])
    y = np.concatenate([np.zeros(n, int), np.ones(n, int)])
    order = np.random.default_rng(seed + 100).permutation(y.size)
    keep = int(0.7 * y.size)
    return X[order[:keep]], y[order[:keep]], X[order[keep:]], y[order[keep:]]

def vote(X_train, y_train, X_query, k):
    out = []
    for row in X_query:
        gap = ((X_train - row) ** 2).sum(axis=1)
        out.append(np.bincount(y_train[np.argsort(gap)[:k]]).argmax())
    return np.array(out)

    for row in X_query:

lessons.title: Delete the Feature and Look Again
lessons.goal: Measure the classifier with both columns, with each column alone, and with one column shuffled.
lessons.theory:
The most useful test in this course takes three lines: **remove a piece and see whether the output changes**. If it does not, that piece was never doing anything, whatever the diagram says.

Here the piece is a feature column. RMS alone barely beats a coin, because both classes carry the same payload distribution and RMS is mostly payload. High frequency energy alone does better and is still poor for the same reason. Together they are strong, because the classifier can compare them against each other and read off the excess chatter per amp. Neither column is the answer and their combination is.

The fourth measurement is the control. Shuffle the second column so it keeps its distribution and loses its pairing with the rows, and the accuracy has to fall back to the single column number. If it does not fall, the second column was never contributing and you have found a bug, not a feature.
lessons.task: Run the classifier four times on the same split: both columns, column zero alone, column one alone, and both columns with the second one shuffled by `np.random.default_rng(5).permutation(X_train.shape[0])`, printing that last one under the caption `second column shuffled`.

lessons.title: What Every Answer Costs
lessons.goal: Count the distance computations and stored numbers a neighbour model needs, and compare against a two prototype model.
lessons.theory:
Nearest neighbour has no training cost and an inference cost proportional to the size of the training set. Every query walks all 420 stored rows. On a robot controller that answers once per window at 5 Hz that is fine. On the same controller running a 200 kHz current loop it is not, and the arithmetic tells you which situation you are in before you write the firmware.

Count two things. **Distance computations per answer** is the number of training rows, and it does not shrink as the model improves. **Stored numbers** is rows times columns, and that memory has to live somewhere on the target.

The cheap alternative is a **prototype** model: keep one average row per class and compare against those. Two distances per answer instead of 420, four stored numbers instead of 840. On this problem it costs more than twenty points, because a single average per class cannot express a boundary that runs diagonally through a cloud both classes share, and on a well separated problem it costs almost nothing. That is a trade a control engineer should make deliberately, after measuring it, rather than by default.
lessons.task: Build the two class prototypes with `X_train[y_train == label].mean(axis=0)`, classify by which prototype is closer, and print the `prototype model accuracy` next to the distance count and the stored number count of that model.

lessons.title: The Right to Refuse
lessons.goal: Reject a query whose nearest training row is further away than a radius taken from the training distances.
lessons.theory:
A classifier with two labels answers one of two labels, always, including when the window in front of it is a kind of failure nobody recorded. A cracked gearbox tooth produces a window that sits nowhere near either class, and the model reports worn with total confidence because worn is marginally closer.

The fix is a **reject option**. Measure how far a typical training row sits from its own nearest neighbour, take a high percentile of that as a radius, and refuse to answer when the closest training row is beyond it. The model then has three outputs: healthy, worn, and unknown.

On a real cell, unknown routes to a human. That is not a failure of the model, it is the model doing the most valuable thing it can do, which is to know the edge of what it was taught. Measure the two things that matter: accuracy on the queries it did answer, and how many of the novel windows it correctly refused.
lessons.task: Take the radius as `np.percentile(own, 99)` over the training distances, then print how many of the novel rows were refused and the `accuracy on the answered rows` of the known test set.

lessons.title: Ninety Six Percent of Nothing
lessons.goal: Compare a trained detector against a constant predictor on a log where faults are four percent of the rows.
lessons.theory:
This log holds 1260 windows and 60 of them are faulty. That is four percent, which is a realistic and even generous fault rate for a machine that is still running. On a set shaped like this, accuracy stops being informative.

A predictor that answers healthy to everything scores 0.952 on the test rows. It has never been fitted, it holds no parameters, and it will never once warn you about a bearing. Any real model has to be compared against that number rather than against zero, and a real model that lands near it has produced nothing.

The deeper problem is that accuracy weights both mistakes the same. Calling a healthy window faulty costs an unnecessary inspection. Calling a faulty window healthy costs a gearbox. Accuracy adds them up as if they were the same event, so the rest of this chapter takes the two mistakes apart and looks at them separately.
lessons.task: Score the constant predictor on the test rows, print it under the caption `constant predictor accuracy`, and then print `faults flagged by the model` and the same count for the constant predictor out of the 15 faulty test windows.

lessons.title: Four Numbers Instead of One
lessons.goal: Build a two by two confusion matrix from predictions and true labels with boolean masks.
lessons.theory:
Every prediction on a two class problem falls into one of four boxes. **True negative**: healthy window called healthy. **False positive**: healthy window called faulty, an inspection nobody needed. **False negative**: faulty window called healthy, the one that costs a gearbox. **True positive**: faulty window called faulty.

Those four counts are the confusion matrix and they contain everything. Accuracy is the diagonal over the total, and it throws away the distinction between the two off diagonal boxes on its way. Once you have the four numbers you can compute every metric in this chapter without going back to the data.

In numpy each box is one boolean expression combined with `&`, counted with `np.count_nonzero`. Write them in the same order every time and read the matrix the same way every time: rows are what was true, columns are what was said.

lessons.title: Precision and Recall
lessons.goal: Compute precision and recall from the confusion boxes and say which question each one answers.
lessons.theory:
**Recall** is the share of real faults the model caught: true positives over all faulty rows. It is the number a maintenance engineer cares about, because a fault the model missed is a fault that keeps running until something breaks.

**Precision** is the share of the alarms that were real: true positives over everything the model called faulty. It is the number the shift supervisor cares about, because every false alarm sends a technician to a healthy machine, and three of those in a row means the next real alarm gets ignored.

They pull against each other. Lower the threshold and you catch more faults and raise more false alarms: recall up, precision down. There is no setting that maximises both, which is why a single number cannot describe a detector and why any report that gives you only accuracy is hiding the trade it made.

lessons.title: Why the Average of the Two Lies
lessons.goal: Compare the arithmetic mean of precision and recall against their harmonic mean on a detector that fires once.
lessons.theory:
Take a detector so cautious it raises exactly one alarm in the whole test set, and that alarm is correct. Precision is 1.000, perfect. Recall is 0.067, because it found one fault out of fifteen. Average the two the ordinary way and you get 0.533, which sounds like a working detector and describes something useless.

The **F1 score** is the harmonic mean, and on the same detector it returns 0.125. A harmonic mean is pulled down hard by its smallest input, which is exactly the behaviour you want: a detector is only as good as its weaker side. Put the cautious detector next to an ordinary one that catches two thirds of the faults and the two plain means land within five hundredths of each other while the two F1 scores differ by a factor of four.

F1 is a summary and it still hides the trade. Report it next to precision and recall rather than instead of them, and never let it be the only number in a report, because two detectors with the same F1 can behave completely differently on a factory floor.

lessons.title: The Two Mistakes Do Not Cost the Same
lessons.goal: Choose between two thresholds by expected cost using a cost per false alarm and a cost per missed fault.
lessons.theory:
Put money on the two mistakes and the choice of threshold stops being a matter of taste. An unnecessary inspection on this cell costs about 120 units of technician time. A missed bearing failure costs about 9000 units in a seized joint, a stripped harmonic drive and half a shift of downtime.

Expected cost is then `fp * COST_ALARM + fn * COST_MISS`, and the threshold that minimises it is usually far below the 0.5 that everyone reaches for by default. With a ratio of 75 to 1, a detector should be willing to raise many false alarms to avoid one miss.

This is where a machine learning result becomes an engineering decision. The model produces a score, the cost structure of the cell decides where to cut it, and those are two separate pieces of knowledge held by two different people. Write both down in the report.
lessons.task: Compute the cost of each candidate threshold with `fp * COST_ALARM + fn * COST_MISS`, print one line per candidate, and print which one wins under the caption `cheapest threshold`.

lessons.title: Sweeping the Threshold
lessons.goal: Trace precision and recall across the whole range of thresholds and read the trade off from the table.
lessons.theory:
The model does not output a decision, it outputs a **score**. Here the score is the fraction of the fifteen nearest training windows that were faulty, so it lives on a grid between 0 and 1. The decision only appears when you compare that score against a threshold, and that comparison is yours to set.

Sweeping the threshold from low to high traces the whole family of detectors the same model can be. At a very low threshold everything is an alarm: recall 1.0, precision near the fault rate. At a very high one nothing is: precision 1.0 or undefined, recall 0. Every useful operating point sits between those two.

Printing the sweep as a table is worth more than any single summary number, because it lets whoever owns the cell point at the row they can live with. Two of the columns are already decided elsewhere: how many technician visits per week the shift can absorb, and how many missed faults the plant will tolerate.
lessons.task: Inside the loop write `precision = tp / (tp + fp) if tp + fp else 1.0` and `recall = tp / (tp + fn) if tp + fn else 0.0`, then print a table with one row per threshold including the alarm count.

lessons.title: Accuracy per Class
lessons.goal: Compute the recall of each class separately and average them into a balanced accuracy.
lessons.theory:
Plain accuracy weights each row equally, so on a set that is 95 percent healthy it is a report about healthy windows with a rounding error attached. **Balanced accuracy** weights each class equally instead: compute the recall of each class and average those.

On the constant predictor the difference is total. Recall on the healthy class is 1.000, recall on the faulty class is 0.000, and the balanced accuracy is exactly 0.500, which is the correct description of a model that knows nothing. Plain accuracy called the same model 0.952.

The per class recalls are worth printing even when you also report the average, because the average can hide an asymmetry that matters. A detector at 0.80 and 0.70 and one at 0.99 and 0.51 have the same balanced accuracy and belong in different factories.

lessons.title: Three Faults and a Square Table
lessons.goal: Build a three by three confusion matrix and find which pair of classes the model confuses.
lessons.theory:
The cell logs three states now: healthy, a worn bearing, and a loose belt. A loose belt raises the average current because the drive has to fight the slip, and it raises the high frequency content a little as well, so it shares part of its signature with a worn bearing.

With three classes the table is three by three and the interesting information is entirely off the diagonal. A model can hold a decent overall accuracy while pouring one whole class into one particular wrong box, and that is a different engineering problem from a model that is uniformly mediocre: it means those two states need a feature that tells them apart, not that the classifier needs tuning. The table names the pair for you, and on this log the answer is not the pair most people guess.

Building the table is one nested loop and no special cases. `matrix[a, b]` counts the rows whose true class is `a` and whose predicted class is `b`, so the diagonal is what went right and every other cell names a specific mistake.
lessons.task: Fill the matrix with `np.count_nonzero((y_test == a) & (guess == b))`, print it row by row, print the largest off diagonal cell under the caption `worst confusion`, and close with the `majority baseline on three classes`.

import numpy as np

def parts(n, kind, rng):
    load = rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, n)
    rms_db = 3.0 + 0.9 * load + rng.normal(0.0, 0.18, n)
    hf_db = 1.0 + 0.9 * load + rng.normal(0.0, 0.18, n)
    if kind == 1:
        hf_db = hf_db + 0.60
    if kind == 2:
        rms_db = rms_db + 0.70
        hf_db = hf_db + 0.30
    return np.column_stack([rms_db, hf_db])

def three_class_log():
    gen = np.random.default_rng(23)
    blocks = [parts(400, kind, gen) for kind in (0, 1, 2)]
    X = np.vstack(blocks)
    y = np.concatenate([np.full(400, kind) for kind in (0, 1, 2)])
    order = np.random.default_rng(77).permutation(y.size)
    keep = int(0.7 * y.size)
    return X[order[:keep]], y[order[:keep]], X[order[keep:]], y[order[keep:]]

    return np.array(out)

lessons.title: The Report That Does Not Hide Anything
lessons.goal: Print one block holding the baseline, the confusion boxes, precision, recall, balanced accuracy and the threshold.
lessons.theory:
Everything in this chapter goes into one block, printed by one function, so that no result of yours ever travels as a single number without its context.

The minimum honest report has five parts. What the majority baseline was, so the reader knows the floor. The four confusion counts, so any metric can be recomputed. Precision and recall, so the trade is visible. Balanced accuracy, so an imbalanced set cannot flatter the model. And the threshold, because a different threshold is a different detector and the report describes one of them.

Write it once and call it from every project. The value of a fixed format is that a number that has drifted becomes obvious next to the others, and that anybody reading it can tell within ten seconds whether the model is better than saying nothing.
lessons.task: Complete the report so it also prints the baseline, then precision and recall, then the `balanced accuracy`, and finish the file with a second call `report(scores, y_test, 0.15)` on the same scores.

lessons.title: When the Answer Is a Temperature
lessons.goal: Set up a regression target and measure the error of the mean predictor in the units of the target.
lessons.theory:
Classification asks which of a few states a window belongs to. **Regression** asks for a number: how many degrees the winding of joint 3 will rise, how many millimetres of backlash the gearbox has, how many minutes of battery are left. The features look the same, the target changes from a small integer to a float, and every metric in chapter 4 stops applying.

The metric that replaces accuracy is **root mean squared error**. Square each miss, average the squares, take the root. The squaring punishes a single large miss more than several small ones, and the root brings the number back into the units of the target, so an RMSE of 4.1 means the model is typically about four degrees off. That is a sentence an engineer can act on.

The baseline changes too. Instead of the majority class it is the **mean of the training targets**, predicted for every row. It is the number to beat and it is not zero: on this log it lands near 16 degrees of error, because the temperature rise spans more than eighty degrees and the mean sits in the middle of that span.

lessons.title: The Column of Ones
lessons.goal: Build a design matrix with a leading column of ones so the fitted line can leave the origin.
lessons.theory:
A linear model computes `linear(X, w)`, a weighted sum of the columns. With two feature columns that expression can only produce planes that pass through the origin, which means a joint drawing zero current at zero duty must be predicted at exactly zero degrees of rise. Sometimes true, usually not.

The fix is a column of ones. Its weight is added to every prediction regardless of the features, which is exactly what an intercept is, and it costs nothing beyond one extra column in the matrix. `np.column_stack` with `np.ones(n)` in front is the whole construction.

Keep the intercept in position zero and keep it there forever. Every function that reads a weight vector afterwards, including the deployment code in chapter 9, has to agree about which position means what. A design matrix whose column order is documented once and never changed is worth more than a clever one.
