lessons.title: Solving for the Weights
lessons.goal: Fit a linear model with least squares and predict the test targets with a matrix product.
lessons.theory:
Least squares picks the weight vector that minimises the sum of the squared residuals. There is a closed form, the normal equations, and numpy exposes a numerically better version of it as `np.linalg.lstsq`, which handles a rank deficient matrix instead of exploding on it.

Call it with the design matrix and the training targets, pass `rcond=None` so it uses the modern cut off rather than a deprecated one, and take the first element of what it returns: that is the weight vector. Prediction is then `linear(A, w)`, one matrix product, no loop.

Fit on the training rows only. Every warning in chapter 0 applies here with the target being a float instead of a label, and it is even easier to miss, because a regression that has seen its test targets does not produce a suspicious 1.000, it produces a plausible looking error that happens to be too small.
lessons.task: Solve for the weights with `np.linalg.lstsq(A_train, y_train, rcond=None)[0]`, predict both sets with the weighted sum helper, and print the training error next to the held out error.
lessons.hint: `np.linalg.lstsq` returns four things, so the weights need the index zero on the end, and the prediction for either set is that matrix combined with the weights.

lessons.title: Reading the Residuals
lessons.goal: Compute residuals on held out rows and find the structure a plain linear model leaves behind.
lessons.theory:
A **residual** is the truth minus the prediction, one number per row, in degrees. The set of residuals holds more information than the RMSE that summarises them, and looking at it is how you find out what the model is missing.

The test is whether the residuals still depend on anything. Sort the held out rows by current, split them into a low group and a high group, and average the residual inside each. For a model that has captured the relationship those two averages are both near zero. For this one they are not, because winding heat goes with the **square** of current and a straight line cannot bend.

That is a diagnosis, not a defect to be tuned away. Residuals that carry structure tell you which term is missing from the model, and the term the physics names here is the one the next lesson adds.
lessons.task: Compute `residual = y_test - linear(A_test, w)`, split the test rows on the median current, and print the mean residual of the low current group next to the `mean residual, high current rows`.

lessons.title: R Squared and Its Negative Half
lessons.goal: Compute the coefficient of determination on training and held out rows and interpret a negative value.
lessons.theory:
R squared reports the share of the variance the model explains: one minus the sum of squared residuals over the sum of squared deviations from the mean. At 1.0 the model is exact, at 0.0 it is exactly as good as predicting the mean.

Below zero it is **worse** than predicting the mean, and that is not a broken formula. On training rows R squared cannot go negative, because least squares would have chosen the mean instead. On held out rows it can, and when it does it is telling you the model has fitted something that does not exist outside its training set.

So report it on held out rows and never on training rows. An R squared of 0.98 quoted without saying which rows it came from is the most common way a regression result gets oversold, and it costs nothing to state the slice next to the number.

    rise = 2.4 * current ** 2 * duty + 3.0 * duty + rng.normal(0.0, 2.5, n)
    return np.column_stack([current, duty]), rise

def thermal_split(seed=6, n=400):
    gen = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    X, y = thermal_log(n, gen)
    keep = int(0.7 * n)
    return X[:keep], y[:keep], X[keep:], y[keep:]

def linear(A, w):
    return (A * w).sum(axis=1)

X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test = thermal_split()

def design(X):
    return np.column_stack([np.ones(X.shape[0]), X])

A_train, A_test = design(X_train), design(X_test)
w = np.linalg.lstsq(A_train, y_train, rcond=None)[0]
wrong = np.array([0.0, 22.0, -40.0])

lessons.title: Putting the Physics in the Matrix
lessons.goal: Add a squared and an interaction column to the design matrix and measure the drop in held out error.
lessons.theory:
Least squares fits a **linear combination of columns**, and nobody said the columns have to be the raw measurements. Copper losses go as current squared times the fraction of time the joint is energised, so a column holding `current ** 2 * duty` describes the heat directly and the fit stays linear in the weights.

This is the cheapest kind of modelling there is and it is where domain knowledge enters. A neural network would have to discover that shape from data; you already know it from the resistance of a winding. Writing it as a column is not a trick, it is putting the physics where the solver can use it.

Measure the result on held out rows, in degrees, against the previous model. If the new column belongs there the error falls a long way and the residual structure from two lessons ago disappears. If it does not, the error barely moves and you have learned something about the machine instead.
lessons.task: Build the wide design matrix with the extra column `X[:, 0] ** 2 * X[:, 1]`, fit it, and print the held out error of both models, the mean residual of the high current group under the new one, and the `weight on the physical term`.
lessons.hint: The weight the solver puts on the new column comes out close to the constant that generated the data, which is the sign that the column is the right shape rather than a lucky one.

lessons.title: The Degree That Went Too Far
lessons.goal: Sweep polynomial degree on twelve training points and watch training error and held out error separate.
lessons.theory:
Give a model enough freedom and it will fit the noise. With twelve training points and a polynomial of degree nine the fit passes almost exactly through every one of them: training error falls towards zero and it means nothing at all.

The held out error tells the other half of the story. It falls while the extra degrees are buying real curvature, reaches a minimum where the model matches the physics, and then climbs steeply as the curve starts to swing wildly between the training points in order to touch them all. Printing both columns side by side is the clearest picture of **overfitting** you will get.

The cure is not always a smaller degree. More data pushes the turning point to the right, and the regularization in the next lesson keeps the degree and shrinks the swings. But the diagnosis always starts with the same two columns, and a report showing only the first one is not a report.
lessons.task: For each degree fit on the twelve training points, measure `rmse(y_test, linear(powers(x_test, degree), w))` next to the training error, and then print the degree with the smallest held out error under the caption `best degree`.
lessons.hint: The powers helper rescales the current before raising it, so the same weights apply to the test currents only if you call it with the same degree on both sets.

lessons.title: Holding the Weights Down
lessons.goal: Add a ridge penalty to the normal equations and recover a usable degree nine fit.
lessons.theory:
The degree nine fit failed because its weights grew enormous, hundreds or thousands in size, with neighbouring terms cancelling each other to squeeze the curve through twelve points. **Ridge regression** adds a penalty on the size of those weights, so the solver has to buy every unit of weight with a reduction in residual.

The closed form is short. Build the matrix of dot products between the columns of the design matrix, which `gram` does with `np.einsum("ij,ik->jk", A, A)`, add the penalty along its diagonal, and solve that system against the same right hand side least squares uses. `np.linalg.solve` does the solving without ever forming an explicit inverse. The identity gets a zero in position zero so the intercept stays unpenalised, since shrinking the intercept just biases every prediction.

The penalty strength is a hyperparameter and it belongs to the validation set, exactly like k did. Sweeping it here on the held out rows is a demonstration, not a protocol. In chapter 7 you will choose it properly and the number will be a little worse and true.
lessons.task: Complete the ridge solver with `np.linalg.solve(gram(A) + lam * eye, (A * y[:, None]).sum(axis=0))`, sweep the penalty, and after the table print one line saying the `largest weight falls from` its value at no penalty to its value at a penalty of one tenth.
lessons.hint: At a penalty of zero the system is the plain normal equations, so that first row has to reproduce the degree nine disaster from the previous lesson before the rest of the sweep means anything.

lessons.title: Weights With Units
lessons.goal: Read the fitted coefficients of the physical model against the constants that generated the data.
lessons.theory:
A weight in a linear model has units, and the units tell you what the number means. In this model the target is degrees and the physical column is amps squared times duty, so its weight is measured in degrees per amp squared per unit duty. That is a thermal resistance in disguise and a motor engineer can argue with it.

That argument is the point. A model whose coefficients you can check against a datasheet is a model you can defend in a design review, and a model that fits well with a coefficient of the wrong sign is a warning that something upstream is wrong: a swapped sensor, a mislabelled column, or a feature that is standing in for something else.

The log here was generated with 2.4 degrees per amp squared per unit duty and 3.0 degrees per unit duty. Fit the model and read the weights against those two numbers. They will not match exactly, because the noise is real, and they will be close enough that you can tell the model found the physics rather than a coincidence.
lessons.task: Fit with `np.linalg.lstsq(physical(X_train), y_train, rcond=None)[0]`, print each weight next to the constant that generated it starting with the `degrees per amp squared per unit duty`, and print the held out error and R squared of the fit.
lessons.solution:
import numpy as np

def thermal_log(n, rng):
    current = rng.uniform(1.0, 6.0, n)
    duty = rng.uniform(0.2, 1.0, n)
    rise = 2.4 * current ** 2 * duty + 3.0 * duty + rng.normal(0.0, 2.5, n)
    return np.column_stack([current, duty]), rise

def thermal_split(seed=6, n=400):
    gen = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    X, y = thermal_log(n, gen)
    keep = int(0.7 * n)
    return X[:keep], y[:keep], X[keep:], y[keep:]

def linear(A, w):
    return (A * w).sum(axis=1)

X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test = thermal_split(seed=9, n=600)

def physical(X):
    return np.column_stack([np.ones(X.shape[0]), X[:, 0] ** 2 * X[:, 1], X[:, 1]])

def rmse(truth, guess):
    return float(np.sqrt(np.mean((truth - guess) ** 2)))

lessons.title: From a Score to a Probability
lessons.goal: Turn a linear score into a probability with the logistic function and read what the shape does.
lessons.theory:
A linear model produces a score that runs from minus infinity to plus infinity. A probability has to live between 0 and 1. The **logistic function**, one over one plus the exponential of the negative score, is the map between them, and it is the only extra piece logistic regression adds to what you built in chapter 5.

Read the shape rather than the formula. At a score of zero it returns exactly 0.5, complete uncertainty. It saturates gently: a score of 3 gives 0.953 and a score of 6 gives 0.998, so pushing the score further stops buying confidence. Its steepest part is around the boundary, which is where a classifier should be most sensitive.

Write it in the stable form. A large negative score sends `np.exp(-z)` to overflow, which produces a warning and then an infinity, so the implementation splits on the sign of the score and uses whichever of the two algebraically identical forms cannot overflow. The version given to you here does that, and every lesson in the chapter uses it.
lessons.task: Write `probabilities = sigmoid(scores)`, print the pairs, and finish with a line captioned `gained between a score of three and a score of six` holding the difference between those two entries.

lessons.title: The Cost of Being Confidently Wrong
lessons.goal: Compute the log loss of a set of probabilities and compare a confident mistake against a hesitant one.
lessons.theory:
Accuracy cannot train a model, because moving a weight by a hair almost never flips a prediction, so the derivative of accuracy is zero nearly everywhere. **Log loss** replaces it: the negative average of the log of the probability the model gave to the correct answer.

It punishes confidence. A model that says 0.99 about a window that turns out faulty pays 4.6. One that says 0.6 about the same window pays 0.51, nine times less, even though both were wrong. That is the behaviour you want from a detector that will be trusted: being unsure is cheap and being certain and wrong is expensive.

The clipping is not cosmetic. A probability of exactly zero on a positive row gives an infinite loss and poisons every average it touches, so the implementation pins the probabilities away from both ends before taking any logarithm.

lessons.title: Which Way Is Downhill
lessons.goal: Compute the gradient of the log loss and check it against a numerical derivative.
lessons.theory:
The gradient of the log loss with respect to the weights is the average over rows of each row's features scaled by that row's error `p - y`, where `p` is the vector of predicted probabilities. It is the same expression least squares would give you if `p` were a linear prediction, which is why logistic regression feels so close to linear regression in code.

Read it as a weighted sum of rows. Each row contributes its own features scaled by its own error, `p - y`. Rows the model already gets right contribute almost nothing, rows it gets badly wrong pull hard, and the sum points in the direction that increases the loss. Moving against it is the whole algorithm.

Never trust a hand derived gradient without checking it. Nudge one weight by a tiny epsilon, measure how the loss changes, divide, and compare against the analytic value. Two numbers that agree to five decimals is the cheapest bug insurance in numerical code, and it catches a transposed matrix or a missing division instantly.

lessons.title: Walking Downhill
lessons.goal: Write the gradient descent loop and watch the loss fall while the held out accuracy rises.
lessons.theory:
The loop is three lines. Start the weights at zero, compute the gradient, step against it by a learning rate, repeat. There is no closed form for logistic regression the way there is for least squares, so this iteration is the fit.

Starting at zero is a real choice and a safe one here. It means the first prediction is 0.5 for every row, the loss starts at 0.693, and the model has no preference until the data gives it one. For a linear model the loss surface has a single minimum, so where you start changes how long the walk takes and not where it ends.

Print the loss every so often rather than only at the end. A loss that falls steeply and then flattens has converged. One that is still falling at the last step means you stopped too early. One that rises means the learning rate is too big, which is the next lesson.
lessons.task: Complete the step with `w = w - rate * gradient(A, y, w)`, run 600 iterations, and print the loss and the held out accuracy at iterations 0, 50, 200 and 600.
lessons.hint: Take the snapshot before the step so that step zero holds the untouched starting weights, whose loss has to come out at the logarithm of two.

value: w = w - rate * gradient(A, y, w)

lessons.title: The Step That Was Too Long
lessons.goal: Run the same fit at four learning rates and identify the one that never converges.
lessons.theory:
The learning rate decides how far each step moves. Too small and the walk takes ten thousand iterations to cover ground a good rate covers in two hundred, which on a real dataset is the difference between a minute and an afternoon.

Too large and the first step overshoots the bottom of the valley and lands far up the other side. The loss jumps to more than ten times where it started, and three hundred steps later it has still not got back down to the value it had before any training happened. The model does not error out, it just wastes the run in a perfectly orderly way, so the only thing that tells you is watching the loss.

Standardized features make the range of safe rates much wider, which is the practical reason chapter 2 came before this one. On raw columns with wildly different spreads the valley is a narrow canyon, and the rate that is stable along the wide direction is far too large along the narrow one.
lessons.task: Run the fit at each rate in `RATES`, print the loss after 5, 40 and 300 steps for each, and print which rates ended above where they started under the caption `rates that diverged`.

lessons.title: What the Weights Say
lessons.goal: Read the sign and size of the fitted weights and check them against the physics of the feature bench.
lessons.theory:
The weights of a logistic model are readable in a way a neighbour model never is. On standardized columns each weight says how many units of score one standard deviation of that feature buys, so their sizes are comparable and their signs are statements about the machine.

Here the fit comes back with a **positive** weight on high frequency energy and a **negative** weight of similar size on RMS. Read that out loud: the model raises its suspicion when the chatter is high **for the current the joint is drawing**. It has discovered the ratio feature from chapter 1 on its own, expressed as a difference in decibels, because it had both columns and a reason to combine them.

That is the check to run on any linear model you fit. If the signs contradict the physics, either the physics is wrong or the pipeline is, and finding out which is more valuable than another point of accuracy.

lessons.title: Is 0.8 Really Eighty Percent
lessons.goal: Group the held out rows by predicted probability and compare each group's predicted rate against its true rate.
lessons.theory:
A logistic model outputs numbers between 0 and 1 and everybody calls them probabilities. Whether they deserve the name is a separate question with its own measurement, and the measurement is a **reliability table**.

Sort the held out rows into bins by predicted probability. Inside each bin, compare the average prediction against the share of rows that were actually faulty. A calibrated model matches them: of the windows it called 0.8, about eighty percent turn out faulty. A model that is confidently wrong in one bin is one you cannot use for a cost calculation, because the expected cost formula from chapter 4 multiplies by those numbers.

Logistic regression trained on log loss usually comes out reasonably calibrated, which is one of its quiet advantages over methods that only produce a score. Check anyway, and check on held out rows, because on training rows the model is calibrated almost by construction.

lessons.title: Three Faults, Three Boundaries
lessons.goal: Fit one logistic model per class against all the others and pick the class with the highest score.
lessons.theory:
Logistic regression answers one yes or no question. With three machine states you fit three of them: healthy against everything else, worn bearing against everything else, loose belt against everything else. That is **one versus rest**, and it is how most linear classifiers handle more than two classes.

Prediction stacks the three scores and takes the largest. Do not compare the probabilities as if they were a distribution over the three classes: each one was fitted against a different question and they do not add up to one. Comparing the raw scores is what the method actually justifies, and normalising them is a separate operation with its own name.

Each fit sees the same feature matrix with a different label vector, built by `(y == kind).astype(int)`. That one line is the whole difference between the three models, which is why this scales to any number of states without new machinery.

lessons.title: The Fault a Straight Line Cannot See
lessons.goal: Fit a linear model on a fault defined by disagreement between two sensors, then add the product column.
lessons.theory:
This joint is driven by two motors, each with its own current sensor, and the fault is a **cross coupled harness**. When the wiring is right both readings deviate together, because they share the payload. When two connectors are swapped they deviate in opposite directions: one reads above nominal exactly when the other reads below.

So the label depends on whether the two deviations have the same sign, and no straight line in the plane of the two readings can separate that. The faulty rows occupy two opposite quadrants and the healthy rows occupy the other two. A linear model on those two columns lands at the baseline and no amount of training fixes it, because the shape it can express is wrong.

Add a column holding the **product** of the two deviations and the problem becomes linear again in the new space: the product is negative exactly when the signs disagree. This is the same move as the squared current term in chapter 5, and it is the honest answer to the question of what a linear model can and cannot do.

lessons.title: One Split Is One Measurement
lessons.goal: Repeat the same fit over thirty random splits and measure how far the reported accuracy moves.
lessons.theory:
You have been reporting a single held out accuracy for six chapters. That number is a **measurement**, and like any measurement made on a finite sample it has a spread. Change the seed of the shuffle and nothing about the model or the data changes, yet the number moves.

How far it moves is worth knowing before you argue about a change that gained two points. Run the identical protocol over thirty seeds and look at the smallest and the largest result. On this dataset with 180 test rows the range spans several points, so a two point improvement is inside the noise and proves nothing on its own.

The spread shrinks as the test set grows, roughly with the square root of its size. That is the real reason to want more data: not to train a better model, but to be able to tell whether you have one.

lessons.title: Every Row Gets a Turn
lessons.goal: Split the data into five folds, train on four and score on the fifth, and average the results.
lessons.theory:
A single split throws away most of your measurement. Seventy percent of the rows are never scored and thirty percent are never trained on. **k fold cross validation** fixes both: cut the shuffled rows into k blocks, and run k experiments where each block takes a turn as the held out set.

Every row is scored exactly once, by a model that did not see it. The average of the k scores uses the whole dataset as a test set, which is why it moves far less between seeds than a single split does. Five folds is the usual compromise: ten gives a slightly better estimate for twice the compute.

The implementation is `np.array_split` on a shuffled index array, then a loop that concatenates every fold except the current one. Nothing else changes: the fit and the score are the same two lines you already have.
lessons.task: Inside the loop build the training index as `np.concatenate([blocks[j] for j in range(FOLDS) if j != i])`, fit, score that fold, print each fold score, and print their mean as the `cross validated accuracy`.

lessons.title: The Number and Its Error Bar
lessons.goal: Report a cross validated accuracy with the spread across folds and compare two models with it.
lessons.theory:
The five fold scores are five measurements of the same quantity, so their standard deviation is an estimate of how uncertain the average is. Reporting the mean without it invites the reader to believe digits that are not there.

Use it to decide whether a change is real. Model A at 0.912 with a fold spread of 0.021 and model B at 0.926 with a spread of 0.019 are not distinguishable by this experiment. Saying so is a result. Quietly shipping B and claiming an improvement is not.

The fold spread understates the true uncertainty, because the k training sets overlap heavily and the scores are therefore correlated. Treat it as a floor on the uncertainty rather than a confidence interval, and when a decision really matters, repeat the whole cross validation with a different shuffle and look at both spreads.

lessons.title: Choosing the Penalty Inside the Training Set
lessons.goal: Select the ridge penalty by cross validation on the training rows and report on a test set never touched.
lessons.theory:
Cross validation replaces the validation slice from chapter 2, and it comes with the same rule attached. The **test set is set aside first**, before any folds exist, and it is opened once at the end.

So the shape of an honest experiment is: split off the test rows, cross validate over the remaining rows to rank the candidate penalties, refit on all the training rows with the winner, score the test rows once. Four steps and the order is not negotiable.

The number you report is the last one. The cross validated score of the winner is usually a little higher, for the winner's curse reason from chapter 2, and it belongs in the report as the selection evidence rather than as the result.

lessons.title: The Learning Curve
lessons.goal: Plot accuracy against training set size as a table and read whether more data would still help.
lessons.theory:
A **learning curve** answers a question a single accuracy cannot: would collecting more windows help. Train on 20 rows, then 40, then 80, all the way up, scoring each model on the same held out set, and read the shape.

A curve that is still climbing at the largest size you have says the model is starved and another week of logging is the cheapest improvement available. A curve that flattened two hundred rows ago says more of the same data is worthless and the next gain has to come from a better feature or a different model.

This is the measurement that decides where the effort goes, and it is nearly free: you already have the data and the fit. Averaging over a few different subsets at each size takes the jitter out and costs nothing but a loop.

lessons.title: Folds That Respect the Machine
lessons.goal: Build folds out of whole robots and compare the result against folds built out of rows.
lessons.theory:
Chapter 2 held out whole arms once. Cross validation has to do the same thing k times, and the version that ignores it is one of the most common broken pipelines in industrial machine learning.

**Grouped k fold** assigns groups to folds instead of rows. Every window of arm 5 lands in the same block, so when that block is held out no row from arm 5 is anywhere in the training set. The score you get answers the question the plant actually asked: how will this behave on the arm we have not instrumented yet.

The two numbers on this data differ by a wide margin, and the honest one is the low one. When a report shows a cross validated score without saying what the folds were made of, that is the question to ask first.
lessons.task: Build the grouped folds by keeping the arms where `unit % FOLDS == f` in fold `f`, run cross validation that way too, and print the result under the caption `folds made of whole arms` next to the baseline.

lessons.title: Ask the Data to Prove It Is Not Noise
lessons.goal: Shuffle the labels many times, cross validate each shuffle, and place the real score against that distribution.
lessons.theory:
Here is the test that catches everything else in this chapter when you have missed it. **Break the link between the features and the labels** by shuffling the label vector, then run your entire pipeline on the broken data. Whatever it reports is what your pipeline produces from nothing.

Do it forty times and you have a distribution of scores under the assumption that there is nothing to learn. Your real score either sits far to the right of that cloud or it does not. If it sits inside the cloud, the model has found nothing, no matter how carefully the folds were built.

The fraction of shuffled runs that reached or beat the real score is a **p value**, and it is the most honest single number a machine learning report can carry. It costs forty fits. On a decision worth anything at all, that is nothing.
lessons.task: Inside the loop write `broken = y.copy()`, shuffle it with the run's own generator, cross validate on it, and print the mean and spread of the shuffled scores plus the count of `shuffles that reached the real score`.

        train = np.concatenate([blocks[j] for j in range(FOLDS) if j != i])
        w = fit(A[train], labels[train])
        out.append(accuracy(A[blocks[i]], labels[blocks[i]], w))
    return float(np.mean(out))

real = cross_validate(y)
print("real cross validated accuracy", round(real, 4))

shuffled = []
for run in range(RUNS):
    gen = np.random.default_rng(500 + run)
    broken = y.copy()
    gen.shuffle(broken)
    shuffled.append(cross_validate(broken))

shuffled = np.array(shuffled)
reached = int(np.sum(shuffled >= real))
print("shuffled labels, mean", round(float(shuffled.mean()), 4), "spread", round(float(shuffled.std()), 4))
print("shuffled labels, best of", RUNS, "runs", round(float(shuffled.max()), 4))
print("shuffles that reached the real score", reached, "of", RUNS)

lessons.title: The One Number You Are Allowed to Quote
lessons.goal: Run the full protocol end to end and print the report that carries the result and everything needed to judge it.
lessons.theory:
Everything in this chapter assembles into one function and one printed block. Set the test rows aside. Cross validate the candidates on what is left. Refit with the winner. Open the test set once. Run the shuffled label control. Print all of it together.

The report is not decoration. A reader who sees only 0.91 cannot tell whether the folds respected the arms, whether the penalty was chosen on the test set, or whether 0.91 is what this pipeline produces from noise. A reader who sees the six lines below can tell all three in ten seconds.

This is the block chapter 9 will print at the end of the project, so write it in a form you would be willing to paste into an email to the plant engineer who has to decide whether to trust it.
lessons.task: Print the six lines: rows and split sizes, the candidates with their cross validated scores, the winner, the accuracy on the `test rows, opened once`, the `shuffled label control`, and the majority baseline.

import numpy as np

def bench(n, worn, rng):
    load = rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, n)
    rms_db = 3.0 + 0.9 * load + rng.normal(0.0, 0.15, n)
    hf_db = (1.4 if worn else 1.0) + 0.9 * load + rng.normal(0.0, 0.15, n)
    return np.column_stack([rms_db, hf_db])

def pattern_loft(n=300, seed=5):
    gen = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    X = np.vstack([bench(n, False, gen), bench(n, True, gen)])
    y = np.concatenate([np.zeros(n, int), np.ones(n, int)])
    order = np.random.default_rng(seed + 9).permutation(y.size)
    X, y = X[order], y[order]
    Z = (X - X.mean(axis=0)) / X.std(axis=0)
    return np.column_stack([np.ones(Z.shape[0]), Z]), y

def linear(A, w):
    return (A * w).sum(axis=1)

def sigmoid(z):
    out = np.empty(z.shape, dtype=float)
    high = z >= 0
    out[high] = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-z[high]))
    low = np.exp(z[~high])
    out[~high] = low / (1.0 + low)
    return out

def fit(A, y, lam=0.0, steps=400, rate=0.5):
    w = np.zeros(A.shape[1])
    for _ in range(steps):
        grad = (A * (sigmoid(linear(A, w)) - y)[:, None]).sum(axis=0) / y.size
        grad[1:] = grad[1:] + lam * w[1:]
        w = w - rate * grad
    return w

def accuracy(A, y, w):
    return float(np.mean((sigmoid(linear(A, w)) > 0.5).astype(int) == y))

FOLDS = 5
PENALTIES = (0.0, 0.1, 1.0)
A, y = pattern_loft(n=350, seed=4)
order = np.random.default_rng(6).permutation(y.size)
keep = int(0.75 * y.size)
train_rows, test_rows = order[:keep], order[keep:]
blocks = np.array_split(train_rows, FOLDS)

def cross_validate(labels, lam):
    out = []
    for i in range(FOLDS):
        inner = np.concatenate([blocks[j] for j in range(FOLDS) if j != i])
        w = fit(A[inner], labels[inner], lam=lam)
        out.append(accuracy(A[blocks[i]], labels[blocks[i]], w))
    return float(np.mean(out))

print("rows", y.size, "training", train_rows.size, "test", test_rows.size)

# TODO: rank, refit, open the test set once, then run the control

FOLDS = 5

lessons.title: How Mixed Is This Pile
lessons.goal: Compute the Gini impurity of a set of labels and read what its extremes mean.
lessons.theory:
A tree splits the data into smaller and smaller groups, and it needs a number that says how mixed a group is so it can prefer splits that make groups purer. **Gini impurity** is that number: one minus the sum of the squared class shares.

Read its two ends. A group that is all one class has share 1.0 for that class, so the impurity is zero: nothing left to separate. A two class group split exactly fifty fifty gives 1 minus 0.25 minus 0.25, which is 0.5, the maximum for two classes. Everything useful happens between those.

It is not the only choice. Entropy behaves almost identically and costs a logarithm. Gini is the default in most implementations because it is cheaper and the trees it grows are nearly the same, and because a quantity built out of squares of counts is easy to reason about when a split has three rows in it.
lessons.task: Return `1.0 - (share ** 2).sum()` from the helper, guarding the empty group, then print the impurity of a pure group, a fifty fifty group, a nine to one group and the whole training set.

lessons.title: One Question, Asked Well
lessons.goal: Find the column and threshold whose split lowers the weighted impurity the most.
lessons.theory:
A **decision stump** is a tree with one question in it. Search every column and every candidate threshold, split the rows in two, and score the split by the impurity of the two halves weighted by their sizes. Keep the best.

Weighting by size is what stops the search from cheating. A cut that peels off two pure rows and leaves 418 mixed ones has one perfectly pure side, and it is worthless. The weighted score prices each half by how much of the data it holds, so a split only wins by making most of the rows purer.

The candidate thresholds are percentiles rather than every distinct value. On 420 rows the exhaustive search costs 840 impurity evaluations per column and the nineteen percentile cuts cost nineteen, and the tree that comes out is the same one for any practical purpose. Every serious implementation does some version of this.

Do not expect much from the answer. One question of the form column below threshold barely clears the baseline on this dataset, because the boundary between the two states runs diagonally and no single axis aligned cut crosses it. That is not a bug in the search, it is the shape of what a stump can say, and the next three lessons are about what it takes to fix it.
lessons.task: Score each candidate cut with `(left.sum() * gini(y[left]) + (~left).sum() * gini(y[~left])) / y.size`, keep the smallest, and print the winning column, its threshold and the `stump accuracy on held out rows`.
lessons.solution:
import numpy as np

def bench(n, worn, rng):
    load = rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, n)
    rms_db = 3.0 + 0.9 * load + rng.normal(0.0, 0.15, n)
    hf_db = (1.6 if worn else 1.0) + 0.9 * load + rng.normal(0.0, 0.15, n)
    return np.column_stack([rms_db, hf_db])

def loft(n=300, seed=5):
    gen = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    X = np.vstack([bench(n, False, gen), bench(n, True, gen)])
    y = np.concatenate([np.zeros(n, int), np.ones(n, int)])
    order = np.random.default_rng(seed + 3).permutation(y.size)
    X, y = X[order], y[order]
    keep = int(0.7 * y.size)
    return X[:keep], y[:keep], X[keep:], y[keep:]

CUTS = np.arange(5, 100, 5)

def gini(labels):
    if labels.size == 0:
        return 0.0
    share = np.bincount(labels, minlength=2) / labels.size
    return float(1.0 - (share ** 2).sum())

NAMES = ["rms in decibels", "high frequency in decibels"]
X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test = loft()

def best_split(X, y):
    best_col, best_cut, best_score = None, None, gini(y)
    for col in range(X.shape[1]):
        for cut in np.percentile(X[:, col], CUTS):
            left = X[:, col] <= cut
            if left.sum() == 0 or (~left).sum() == 0:
                continue
            score = (left.sum() * gini(y[left]) + (~left).sum() * gini(y[~left])) / y.size
            if score < best_score:
                best_col, best_cut, best_score = col, float(cut), score
    return best_col, best_cut, best_score

print("impurity before any split", round(gini(y_train), 4))
print("candidate cuts per column", CUTS.size)

col, cut, score = best_split(X_train, y_train)
left = X_train[:, col] <= cut
side = int(np.bincount(y_train[~left], minlength=2).argmax())
guess = np.where(X_test[:, col] <= cut, 1 - side, side)
print("the stump asks about", NAMES[col], "at", round(cut, 3))
print("impurity after the split", round(score, 4))
print("stump accuracy on held out rows", round(float(np.mean(guess == y_test)), 3))
print("baseline", round(max(np.bincount(y_test)) / y_test.size, 3))
lessons.hint: The tilde flips the boolean mask, so the two halves are `left` and `~left` and their sizes add up to the number of rows the split was given.

value: stump accuracy on held out rows

lessons.title: Asking a Second Question
lessons.goal: Recurse the split into both halves and find the depth at which the extra questions start to pay.
lessons.theory:
A tree is the stump applied again to each side. Split the rows, then run the same search inside the left group and inside the right group, and stop when the depth runs out, the group is pure, or too few rows are left to say anything.

A node is a tuple of column, threshold, left subtree and right subtree, and a leaf is just the majority label as a plain integer. That representation is enough to write the predictor as a loop that walks down until it stops finding tuples, and it is small enough to print and read.

The stopping rules matter more than the splitting rule. Without a minimum group size a tree keeps splitting until every leaf holds one row, which is the memorizing model from chapter 0 dressed as a diagram. Depth and minimum rows are the two knobs, and the next lesson measures what they cost.
lessons.task: Complete the recursion with `grow(X[left], y[left], depth - 1)` for the low side and `grow(X[~left], y[~left], depth - 1)` for the high side, then print the accuracy of depth zero through three on the same held out rows.
lessons.hint: Both children are built from the rows on their own side of the cut, so the left call gets `X[left]` and `y[left]` and the right call gets the two masked with the tilde.

lessons.title: How Deep Before It Starts Lying
lessons.goal: Sweep tree depth and read the training and held out curves against a linear model on the same rows.
lessons.theory:
Depth is to a tree what polynomial degree was to a regression. Each extra level doubles the number of leaves the tree can have, and past a point those leaves stop describing the machine and start describing individual windows.

The curves separate exactly the way chapter 7 predicted. Training accuracy climbs towards one and the held out curve rises, flattens and then sags. Read the sag as the point where the tree began carving out regions that exist only in the training sample.

There is a second lesson in the same table. Every question a tree asks is of the form column below threshold, so the regions it can draw are rectangles with sides parallel to the axes. The boundary in this dataset is a diagonal, and a stack of rectangles approximating a diagonal needs a lot of depth to do badly what the logistic model of chapter 6 did with three numbers. Print that number in the same table and the comparison is unavoidable.
lessons.task: For each depth print the training accuracy, then `tree_accuracy(node, X_test, y_test)` and their gap, and close with a line captioned `logistic model with three numbers`.
lessons.hint: The tree scores are computed by the same helper on two different sets, and the logistic line is there to show that depth is buying you back something a straight boundary had for free.

lessons.title: A Forest of Unstable Trees
lessons.goal: Train many deep trees on bootstrap samples and take a majority vote across them.
lessons.theory:
A deep tree is **unstable**: change a handful of training rows and the split at the root can move, which rewrites the whole tree below it. That sounds like a fatal flaw and it is the property that makes the next trick work.

**Bagging** trains many trees, each on a bootstrap sample, meaning a sample of the same size drawn with replacement. Each tree sees a slightly different dataset, makes different mistakes, and the majority vote across them cancels a good share of those mistakes. What survives the vote is the structure that showed up in most of the samples, which is another way of saying the structure that is really there.

The vote helps only because the trees disagree. Twenty copies of the same tree vote exactly like one tree. That is why the individual trees are grown deep and unpruned: their instability is the source of the diversity the ensemble is spending.
lessons.task: Draw each bootstrap sample with `gen.integers(0, y_train.size, y_train.size)`, grow a deep tree on it, collect the votes, and print the mean accuracy of the individual trees next to `the vote of all of them`.
lessons.hint: Drawing integers with replacement means some rows appear twice and about a third never appear at all, and that last line measures exactly how large that third is.

value: the vote of all of them

lessons.title: Which Column Is Carrying the Model
lessons.goal: Measure feature importance by breaking one column at a time and watching the held out accuracy fall.
lessons.theory:
**Permutation importance** is the erasure test from chapter 3 turned into a routine. Take the fitted model, shuffle one column of the held out set so it keeps its distribution and loses its pairing with the rows, and measure how far the accuracy drops. Repeat for each column.

It beats counting how often a tree splits on a column, because that count measures what the fitting procedure liked rather than what the model needs. It also works on any model at all, including one you did not write, which makes it the right tool for auditing something a vendor shipped you.

Run each column a few times with different shuffles and average, because one shuffle is one noisy measurement. A column whose importance is zero within that noise can be removed, and removing it is worth doing: fewer columns means less to instrument, less to calibrate and less to go wrong on the robot.
lessons.task: For each column, shuffle only that column of a copy of the test matrix with `gen.permutation(broken[:, col])`, average the drop over five shuffles, print one line per column, and then repeat the whole measurement on a matrix with a third column of pure noise so you can see what `a column of pure noise drops`.
lessons.hint: Assigning into `broken[:, col]` replaces one column in place, and the copy is what keeps the real test matrix intact for the next round of the loop.

value: a column of pure noise drops

lessons.title: Learning to Drive by Watching
lessons.goal: Fit a steering policy by least squares on a log of human demonstrations and measure its action error.
lessons.theory:
**Behaviour cloning** is supervised learning where the target is what a person did. An operator drives the corridor robot with a joystick, the controller logs the state and the commanded steering rate at 20 Hz, and you fit a model from state to command. Nothing about the method is new: it is chapter 5 with a different meaning attached to the columns.

The state here is two numbers, the lateral offset from the corridor centre line and the heading error, and the action is a steering rate in radians per second. The operator in this log follows a saturating law: proportional near the centre line, and limited to half a radian per second because that is what the drive can deliver.

The metric is the **action error**, the average absolute difference between what the model commands and what the operator commanded, in the units of the actuator. On held out demonstration rows it comes out around three ten thousandths of a radian per second, which sounds like a finished job and is the setup for the next lesson.
lessons.task: Fit with `np.linalg.lstsq(design(train_log), train_log[:, 2], rcond=None)[0]`, then print the `mean action error on held out demonstrations` and the worst one.
lessons.hint: The design helper already builds the constant column and the two state columns, so the fit is one call and the prediction on any log is the other helper.

value: mean action error on held out demonstrations

lessons.title: The States the Operator Never Visited
lessons.goal: Evaluate the cloned policy far outside the demonstrated envelope and compare its commands against the actuator limit.
lessons.theory:
The held out demonstrations came from the same distribution as the training demonstrations, so the tiny error from the previous lesson only certifies the model inside the envelope the operator stayed in. That envelope is fifteen centimetres wide, because a competent operator does not let the robot wander.

The robot will leave that envelope. A wheel slips on coolant, someone bumps the cart, the localisation jumps, and suddenly the state is three metres off the centre line, which is a state that appears **nowhere** in the training data. This is **covariate shift**: the distribution the policy meets in operation is not the distribution it was fitted on, and no amount of held out validation inside the log can warn you about it.

Here the failure is concrete and physical. The operator's law saturates at half a radian per second. The straight line clone has no such idea, so at three metres off centre it asks for eleven times what the drive can deliver, and everything downstream of that command is running open loop against a saturated actuator.
lessons.task: Roll the expert out from three metres off centre, built as `far = rollout(expert, 3.0, 0.0, 400)`, evaluate the cloned commands along it, and print the mean and worst action error there next to the `largest command the clone asks for` and the actuator limit.
lessons.solution:
import numpy as np

DT, SPEED, LIMIT = 0.05, 1.2, 0.5

def expert(e, h):
    return -LIMIT * float(np.tanh((2.0 * e + 3.0 * h) / LIMIT))

def rollout(policy, e, h, steps):
    log = []
    for _ in range(steps):
        u = policy(e, h)
        log.append((e, h, u))
        h = h + u * DT
        e = e + SPEED * np.sin(h) * DT
    return np.array(log)

def demonstrations(seed, spread, count, steps=120):
    gen = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    rows = [rollout(expert, float(gen.uniform(-spread, spread)), float(gen.uniform(-0.05, 0.05)), steps)
            for _ in range(count)]
    return np.vstack(rows)

def design(log):
    return np.column_stack([np.ones(log.shape[0]), log[:, 0], log[:, 1]])

def commanded(w, log):
    return w[0] + w[1] * log[:, 0] + w[2] * log[:, 1]

log = demonstrations(seed=5, spread=0.15, count=30)
keep = int(0.7 * log.shape[0])
train_log, test_log = log[:keep], log[keep:]
w = np.linalg.lstsq(design(train_log), train_log[:, 2], rcond=None)[0]
print("held out demonstration rows", test_log.shape[0])

inside = rollout(expert, 0.12, 0.0, 200)
inside_error = np.abs(commanded(w, inside) - inside[:, 2])
print("inside the envelope, mean action error", round(float(inside_error.mean()), 5))

far = rollout(expert, 3.0, 0.0, 400)
far_error = np.abs(commanded(w, far) - far[:, 2])
print("outside it, mean action error", round(float(far_error.mean()), 5))
print("outside it, worst action error", round(float(far_error.max()), 4))
print("largest command the clone asks for", round(float(np.abs(commanded(w, far)).max()), 3))
print("largest command the drive can deliver", LIMIT)
lessons.hint: Both errors are measured the same way against the same expert, so the only thing that changed between the two numbers is where the trajectory started.

value: largest command the clone asks for

lessons.title: Bringing the Operator Back
lessons.goal: Add recovery demonstrations from far off states, refit, and measure what the correction costs inside the envelope.
lessons.theory:
The fix for covariate shift is not a better fitting procedure, it is **data from the states the policy will actually meet**. Put the robot three metres off the centre line, hand the joystick back to the operator, log the recovery, and add those rows to the training set. That loop of rolling out, collecting corrections and refitting is the idea behind dataset aggregation.

It works here and it charges for it. Adding recoveries cuts the action error outside the envelope by a large factor, and the same weights now have to serve two regimes with one straight line, so the error inside the envelope rises from three ten thousandths to something you can see. A linear policy cannot be both the gentle law near the centre and the saturated law far out. The correct response is a policy with more shape, trained on the aggregated data.

And the reason this matters on a robot rather than in a notebook: collecting the recovery data means putting real hardware into the state you are afraid of. That is cheap in simulation, expensive on a five tonne AGV, and it is why the next course spends its time on learning that does not require crashing first.
lessons.task: Build `aggregated = np.vstack([log, recovery])`, fit on it, and report that policy under the name `plus recovery runs` next to the one fitted on the demonstrations alone.

lessons.title: Twelve Arms and a Question
lessons.goal: Cut the fleet logs into labelled windows and keep the unit each window came from.
lessons.theory:
The mission for this chapter: twelve arms of the same model have been logged for six seconds each at 1 kHz. Six run a bearing that a technician has confirmed as worn, six are known good. Build a detector that will be installed on an arm nobody has logged yet, and report a number that is worth acting on.

Everything you need is in the previous nine chapters and the only new thing is discipline. The chapter builds one file end to end, in order, and every lesson adds the piece the next one needs. Nothing is thrown away and nothing is measured twice.

The first piece is bookkeeping and it is the one that makes the honest split possible later. Cut each log into windows, and carry three arrays instead of two: the features, the label, and the **unit number**. That third array is what lets chapter 2's grouped split exist at all, and a pipeline that discards it can never be repaired downstream.

lessons.title: The Feature Block
lessons.goal: Reduce every window to three decibel features and check that each one responds to wear.
lessons.theory:
Three features, all in decibels, all from chapter 1. **Level** is the RMS of the raw window, which is dominated by the payload. **Chatter** is the mean absolute step between neighbouring samples, the high frequency proxy. **Wobble** is the RMS after removing the window's own mean, the AC amplitude.

Decibels are not decoration. Load multiplies the signal, and a multiplication becomes an addition once you take twenty times the base ten logarithm. In that space the ratio feature from chapter 1 is a **difference between two columns**, which is exactly the shape a linear model can express with two weights of opposite sign. That is why the logistic model in chapter 6 found it without help.

Check each column before trusting any of them. Print the class means and the gap in decibels. A column whose two class means sit within a tenth of a decibel of each other is carrying nothing, and the one that behaves that way here is the one about payload.
lessons.task: Build the fleet table, then for each column print the healthy mean, `X[y == 1, col].mean()` and the gap between them in decibels, and finish with the `spread inside the healthy class`.

lessons.title: Freezing Four Arms
lessons.goal: Hold out four whole units, fit the scaler on the rest, and prove no unit appears on both sides.
lessons.theory:
The split happens now, before any model exists, and it holds out **whole units**. Arms 8, 9, 10 and 11 are the test fleet: two healthy and two worn, a hundred and twenty windows, and not one of their rows will be seen by anything until the last lesson of this chapter.

The scaler is fitted here too, on the training units only, and the two vectors it holds travel with the model from this point on. A scaler refitted later, or fitted on everything, is the leak from chapter 2 and it is silent.

Print the proof rather than trusting the code. The set of units on the training side and the set on the test side have to be disjoint, both sides have to contain both labels, and the scaled test columns have to come out near zero mean but not at it. Three lines, and they are the difference between a result and a claim.
lessons.task: Take `mu = X[~test].mean(axis=0)` and the matching spread from the training rows only, build the prepared matrix, and print the units on each side, the list of `units on both sides`, the class counts and the scaled column means of both.

lessons.title: Choosing the Penalty on the Fleet
lessons.goal: Cross validate the ridge penalty over folds made of whole training units and refit with the winner.
lessons.theory:
Four candidate penalties, four folds, and every fold is two whole units, one healthy and one worn. The pairing matters: units alternate healthy and worn, so taking them two at a time from an even number gives every fold the same class balance. Folds built by taking every fourth unit would each have held a single class, and a fold with one label in it cannot report an accuracy that means anything.

What this measures is exactly what the plant will experience: a model fitted on some arms, asked about an arm it has never seen. A row level fold would give a higher number here for the reason chapter 7 measured, and that higher number would describe nothing that will ever happen.

The winner is refitted on all eight training units before it goes anywhere near the test fleet. The cross validated score of the winner goes in the report as the selection evidence, not as the result.

lessons.title: The Threshold Is an Engineering Decision
lessons.goal: Collect out of fold probabilities on the training units and pick the alarm threshold that minimises expected cost.
lessons.theory:
The model gives a probability. Turning it into an alarm needs a threshold, and chapter 4 established where that number comes from: the cost of the two mistakes. On this cell an unnecessary inspection costs 120 units and a missed bearing failure costs 9000.

The threshold has to be chosen on data the model did not fit, and the test fleet is still frozen, so the material is the **out of fold probabilities**: for each training unit, the probability the model gave it when that unit was in the held out fold. Every training row gets a probability from a model that never saw it, and the sweep runs on those.

The answer will be far below 0.5, because 9000 divided by 120 is 75 and the arithmetic does not care what the default is. Print the cost curve rather than just its minimum, because a minimum that sits on a cliff is a threshold that will not survive a change in the fleet.
lessons.task: Fill the vector with `out_of_fold[rows] = sigmoid(linear(A[rows], w))`, sweep the candidate thresholds over it, print the cost at each, and print the `chosen threshold` at the end.

lessons.title: The Thing That Ships
lessons.goal: Write the deployment function that takes one raw window and returns healthy, worn or unknown.
lessons.theory:
Everything so far produced numbers. This produces the artefact: a function that takes one window of raw current, straight off the controller, and answers. It carries four frozen things and nothing else. The scaler's two vectors, the weight vector, and the threshold.

It also carries a refusal. Chapter 3 built the reject option and here it earns its place: if the scaled window sits further from the training cloud than any training row did, the answer is **unknown** and a person looks at it. A detector that cannot say unknown will confidently classify a window from a machine state nobody has ever recorded.

Read the shape of the function and notice what is missing. No fitting, no labels, no dataset. If any of those appear inside the deployment path, the model is being retrained on the robot, and whatever it reports is no longer the thing you validated.

lessons.title: Opening the Frozen Fleet
lessons.goal: Score the finished detector on the four held out arms once and print the report with its controls.
lessons.theory:
The test fleet opens now, for the first and only time. Everything that goes into the report has already been decided: the features, the split, the penalty, the threshold, the radius. Nothing after this line may change any of them, because the moment a choice is made in response to this number, the number stops being a measurement.

The report carries three controls beside the result. The **majority baseline**, because a detector that cannot beat a constant is not a detector. The **shuffled label control** from chapter 7, which tells you what this exact pipeline reports when there is nothing to learn. And an **ablation**, refitting with each feature removed, which tells you whether every column is earning its place.

Accuracy is not the headline here and the report says so by printing two operating points. At the threshold the cost calculation chose, the detector misses nothing and pays for it in unnecessary inspections, so its accuracy is modest and its recall is one. At the neutral threshold of one half the same weights score twenty points higher and let faults through. The plant picks the row, and the two numbers together are what makes that a choice rather than a default.

Read the ablation as the closing argument of the whole course. The column whose class means sat fourteen thousandths of a decibel apart in lesson two, the one about payload and not about wear, is the one whose removal collapses the detector. It was never separating anything by itself: it was the reference the other two were being measured against. Meanwhile the two columns that looked strongest turn out to be interchangeable, and dropping either one costs nothing, which means the shipped detector needs two features rather than three.
